The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644. It built the Forbidden City, sent huge fleets across the Indian Ocean and made blue-and-white porcelain famous. Then, from the 1500s on, it limited sea trade. Why did a rich, sea-going empire pull back? Historians still argue about the answer. The story matters because it shapes how we see China and the world.
Hongwu rebuilds China

Zhu Yuanzhang, once a poor peasant and a Buddhist monk, led the rebels who drove out the Mongol Yuan dynasty. He founded the Ming in 1368 and took the name Hongwu. He restored the civil service exams and ordered new land surveys. Hongwu was suspicious of his own officials and ruled with harsh punishments. His early policies set patterns of control that his successors kept.
Yongle and the new capital

Yongle, Hongwu's son, seized the throne in 1402. He moved the capital north to Beijing and began the Forbidden City in 1406, which was finished around 1420. He also repaired the Grand Canal and sent out the great naval voyages of Zheng He. The Forbidden City has more than 900 buildings, and it was the seat of power for Ming and later Qing emperors. It shows how the Ming wanted to project order and centrality.
Ray Huang and the year 1587

Ray Huang, 1587, A Year of No Significance (1981) Huang chose one ordinary year, 1587, and showed how the Ming state worked from the inside. The emperor stayed away from court, and officials argued over rules, money and power. The book shows that the state had a rigid system, and that small disputes could block big decisions. It helps explain the later caution about the sea.
Ming in key dates
The timeline shows how the state's sea power grew, then pulled back, and then collapsed under rebellion and invasion.
Porcelain and silver

Blue-and-white porcelain was one of the great Chinese exports, sold across the Islamic world and Europe. In exchange, China took in silver from Japan in the 1500s and from the Americas by the 1570s. Spanish galleons from Manila brought Mexican silver to Asia. Silver became the currency of trade. It was also needed for taxes, and the Ming state came to depend on it. That dependency made the empire sensitive to shifts in the silver supply.
Did China shut itself off?

A popular image shows the Ming as isolated, uninterested in the outside world, and closed by a single decree. The phrase "closed door" is used for that picture. Historians argue the reality was messy. Private overseas trade was banned for long periods, but goods still moved through Portuguese ports, Japanese traders and smugglers. The "closed door" was partial and changed over time.
Pirates and the sea ban

From the 1300s onward the Ming banned private overseas trade several times. The aim was to stop pirates, called wokou, who raided the coasts. The ban also helped the state keep control over trade through official tribute missions. Smugglers ignored the bans, and coastal families grew rich on illegal trade. The gap between the law and the market created tensions that grew with time.
The single whip reform

In the 1580s the minister Zhang Juzheng pushed a reform called the single whip. It combined many taxes into one payment, made mainly in silver. It was meant to simplify the system and to cut corruption. The reform made silver central to government, and it tied the empire's finances to global silver flows. When silver supply shifted, the Ming felt it deeply.
Why did the voyages stop?

Zheng He made seven voyages between 1405 and 1433. Historians argue the reasons for stopping them. Some point to cost and to the rise of Confucian officials who distrusted eunuch admirals. Others point to the threat from the Mongol frontier. The question is not only about China. It shows how far a rich state can turn its back on the sea, and how a choice can shape centuries.
Meanwhile in India…

Zheng He's fleets reached the Indian coast. They visited Calicut and Cochin in the early 1400s, and in 1411 they fought the king of Ceylon and took him to China as a prisoner. Calicut was a great pepper port, and Chinese silk and porcelain reached its markets. The Indian Ocean was a busy network of kingdoms, and Ming ships were only one part of it.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Ming ruled from 1368 to 1644. Yongle moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City. Zheng He sailed from 1405 to 1433. Silver reached China from Japan and the Americas. The single whip reform tied taxes to silver. Think about it Was the closed door a choice or a set of responses to problems? How did silver change the power of a state?
The Dutch Golden Age: Tulips, Trade and Tolerance
A small republic with a global reach

In the 1600s the Dutch Republic was a small, new state that ruled the seas. Its traders reached Asia, the Americas and Africa. Its painters, scientists and mapmakers gained fame across Europe. The Dutch Golden Age shows how trade, money and tolerance could create a rich culture. It also shows how fragile such success can be.
Freedom from Spain

The northern provinces of the Low Countries revolted against Spanish rule from 1568. In 1581 they declared independence in the Act of Abjuration. Spain did not fully accept the Dutch Republic until the Peace of Münster in 1648. The war was long and bitter, but the Dutch fought on, using their rivers, canals and fleets. Their state became a federation of provinces ruled by merchant elites.
The VOC and the first share market

The Dutch East India Company, the VOC, was founded in 1602. It was among the first companies to sell shares to the public, and its shares were traded in Amsterdam. It built a trading empire in Asia, with a base at Batavia, now Jakarta. The VOC controlled the spice trade from the Banda Islands and the Moluccas. Its ships sailed around the Cape of Good Hope, and its agents fought wars and signed treaties across the Indian Ocean.
Simon Schama and the embarrassment of riches

Simon Schama, The Embarrassment of Riches (1987) Schama looks at Dutch culture in the 1600s: its art, its anxieties and its sense of guilt about wealth. He argues that the Dutch felt both proud and uneasy about their success. The book is a classic of cultural history, and it shows how a trading society made its own art and ideas.
The Golden Age in key dates
The Golden Age ran from the late 1500s to about the 1670s. Wars with England and France then ended its time at the top.
Rembrandt and Vermeer

Rembrandt painted The Night Watch in 1642. It is a group portrait of a militia company, full of light and movement. Vermeer, from Delft, painted quiet interiors with clear light, such as Girl with a Pearl Earring, from around 1665. Dutch painters sold their work to a large middle-class market. Paintings of ships, flowers and kitchens were in high demand, and this shaped the look of Dutch art.
Did tulip mania ruin the nation?

The story of tulip mania in 1636 and 1637 is often told as a great national crash. People supposedly traded houses for single bulbs and were ruined overnight. Historians such as Anne Goldgar argue the story is greatly exaggerated. The trade was mostly in futures contracts among ordinary people, and the wider economy was not badly harmed. The version we know was made up later, in a 19th-century book.
A city of many faiths

Amsterdam welcomed Jews fleeing Iberia, Protestant refugees and Catholics, although Catholics had fewer rights. The city's tolerance attracted thinkers from across Europe. The philosopher René Descartes lived in the Dutch Republic for years. Baruch Spinoza, born in Amsterdam in 1632, was expelled from the Jewish community in 1656. His ideas on reason and the state were radical, and they still shape debates about freedom of thought.
Lenses, maps and the new science

Anton van Leeuwenhoek of Delft used simple lenses to see tiny living things, including bacteria, in the 1670s. Dutch mapmakers such as Blaeu produced atlases of the world, and Christiaan Huygens studied light and the pendulum clock. Historians argue whether the Dutch were leaders of the scientific revolution or a bridge between old and new ideas. Their trade gave them a constant flow of maps, instruments and specimens.
Wars at sea

The Dutch fought three wars against England, in 1652–1654, 1665–1667 and 1672–1674. They were fought over trade routes, fishing and sea power. The Dutch fleet under Michiel de Ruyter was among the best in Europe. In 1672 the French invaded, and the republic nearly fell. The crisis led to the rise of William III of Orange, who later became king of England.
Meanwhile in India…

The Dutch set up factories on the Indian coast, including Pulicat on the Coromandel coast in 1610 and Masulipatnam earlier. They bought cotton cloth, indigo and saltpetre, and shipped them to Europe and Southeast Asia. Indian textiles were so valued that Dutch ships carried them back to the spice islands. Indian cloth became a key item of Dutch trade, and it helped fund the Golden Age.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The revolt against Spain started in 1568. The VOC was founded in 1602. Rembrandt painted The Night Watch in 1642. Tulip mania is partly a myth. Dutch trading posts in India bought cotton and indigo. Think about it How did tolerance help a trading state? What is the difference between a market boom and a crash?
Tokugawa Japan and the Closed Country
Two centuries of peace behind closed doors

From 1603 to 1868 Japan was ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns. The country had almost no wars for over two hundred years. It limited foreign trade, but it also grew rich, urban and educated. The Tokugawa period is one of the most surprising stories in world history. It shows that a state can shut the door and still build a rich culture.
Sekigahara and the new shogun

In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu won the battle of Sekigahara against rival warlords. He took the title of shogun in 1603 and set up a government in Edo, a fishing village that became a great city. The shogun ruled through the daimyo, the regional lords. He kept them in line with a system of hostages, rules and inspections, which kept the peace for many generations.
Edo: a city of a million

Edo, now Tokyo, grew to about a million people by the 1700s, making it one of the largest cities in the world. The daimyo had to spend time in Edo under the system called sankin-kōtai, or alternate attendance. Their families stayed there as hostages. The system drove the building of roads, inns and castles. It also filled Edo with merchants, craftsmen and entertainers, who created a lively urban culture.
Engelbert Kaempfer in Dejima

Engelbert Kaempfer (1651–1716) A German doctor who worked for the Dutch East India Company, Kaempfer visited Japan in 1690 and 1692. He wrote a detailed history of the country, which was published in English in 1727. His account gave Europe much of its knowledge of Japan for a long time, though it is shaped by the views of a visitor.
The Tokugawa in key dates
The shogunate ended in 1868, when samurai from the south restored imperial rule. The Meiji era then began.
Shimabara and the fear of Christianity

In 1637 and 1638, Christian peasants and former samurai rose in revolt at Shimabara. The shogun's army crushed them, killing many. The revolt led the government to see Christianity as a threat and to ban missionaries. Portuguese traders were expelled in 1639. The Dutch were allowed to stay, but only on the small artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour.
Was Japan completely closed?

Many people think that Japan closed its doors entirely from the 1600s until the arrival of Commodore Perry in 1853. The word "sakoku", or closed country, is often used for that picture. Historians argue the picture is too simple. The term sakoku was coined only in 1801 by the scholar Shizuki Tadao. Trade continued through Dejima, Chinese merchants at Nagasaki, Korea through Tsushima and the Ryukyu islands through the Satsuma domain.
Learning from the Dutch

Through Dejima, Japanese scholars learned about Dutch medicine, astronomy and maps. This study was called rangaku, or Dutch learning. In 1774 a team translated a Dutch anatomy text into Japanese, the Kaitai Shinsho, which shows how serious the work was. Dutch learning helped Japan prepare for the wave of Western power in the 1800s. It also made Japanese doctors and scholars among the best informed in East Asia.
Peace and the samurai

During the peace, samurai became officials and scholars more than soldiers. Neo-Confucian ideas taught order, loyalty and education, and they shaped how the shogunate governed. Historians argue whether the peace made Japan a stable, well-run state or a rigid society held back by its own rules. Both views have force. The peace did produce high literacy and a huge book trade.
Edo culture

Woodblock prints, kabuki theatre and popular novels grew up in Edo and Osaka. The woodblock prints of artists like Hokusai and Hiroshige, from the 1800s, were among the most famous images of Japan. Literacy spread among townspeople, and the Edo book market was one of the largest in the world. Culture was no longer limited to the court.
Meanwhile in India…

The Dutch carried Japanese silver and copper to Asia, and some of it reached India. They used it to buy Indian cotton textiles on the Coromandel and Bengal coasts. So Japanese metal financed Indian weaving, and Indian cloth then went back to Japan. The Tokugawa period shows how a closed country was still part of a global trade system.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Sekigahara in 1600 led to Tokugawa rule. The shogun ruled from Edo, which grew to about a million people. Shimabara (1637–1638) led to a ban on Christianity. The Dutch traded from Dejima. The shogunate ended in 1868. Think about it Can peace be a sign of strength for a state? Was sakoku a policy, or a name given later?
The Enlightenment
Dare to think for yourself

In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered a magazine's question, 'What is Enlightenment?' His answer: it is humans leaving behind their self-imposed laziness in thinking. His motto was Sapere aude , 'Dare to know'. That daring changed kings, churches and the way we vote.
Reason in the cafes

The Enlightenment (roughly the late 1600s to the late 1700s) grew out of the Scientific Revolution. If reason can explain the planets, why not government, religion and trade? Ideas travelled in coffeehouses, salons hosted by clever women in Paris, and print. The huge Encyclopedie of Diderot (1751-72) tried to gather all knowledge.
Four big voices

John Locke ( Two Treatises , 1689): people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and can remove a ruler who breaks the trust. Montesquieu ( The Spirit of the Laws , 1748): separate the powers of government.
The pen is mightier

Voltaire fought for tolerance and attacked religious persecution, after the Calas affair (1762), in which an innocent Protestant was executed. Rousseau ( The Social Contract , 1762) wrote that man is born free but is everywhere in chains, and argued rule should follow the 'general will'. Rousseau and Voltaire disliked each other intensely.
Money and women

Adam Smith , in The Wealth of Nations (1776), argued free markets create wealth. Mary Wollstonecraft wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) and said women need education to be equal. Most Enlightenment writers did not extend 'all men' to women.
Kings who liked ideas

Some rulers, called 'enlightened despots', used reason to reform without sharing power: Frederick the Great of Prussia, Catherine the Great of Russia, Joseph II of Austria. Ideas also lit the revolutions in America and France.
Did Voltaire say 'I disapprove of what you say...'?

Myth: Voltaire said, 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.' Fact: that line was written in 1906 by Evelyn Beatrice Hall, summing up his attitude. He never wrote it. Also, many Enlightenment thinkers held racist views or profited from slavery. Historians argue whether those ideas were part of the Enlightenment or a betrayal of it.
Meanwhile in India…

Reason travels to Calcutta Enlightenment ideas reached British Bengal through the Company's own judges and scholars. William Jones founded the Asiatic Society at Calcutta in 1784. In 1786 he noted that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin shared a common origin, the seed of the Indo-European idea. Charles Wilkins's English Gita appeared in 1785. Indians took up the ideas themselves. Rammohan Roy (1772–1833), who read Locke and Bentham, founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828 and campaigned against sati, banned in 1829. At Hindu College, Henry Derozio's Young Bengal students read Paine and Hume in the 1820s and questioned custom and caste.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Enlightenment thinkers prized reason and evidence. Locke: natural rights; Montesquieu: separation of powers. Voltaire: tolerance; Rousseau: general will. Smith and Wollstonecraft brought economics and women's rights in. Ideas had limits: slavery and empire. Think about it Which Enlightenment idea matters most to you today? Can ideas of freedom be applied unequally?
The American Revolution
The Tea Party was about monopoly, not the price of tea

On 16 December 1773, men dressed as Mohawks boarded three ships in Boston harbour and dumped 342 chests of tea into the water. It looks like a story about a tax. It was really about a company. The company was the East India Company, and it ties directly to us.
Taxes and a lost war

Britain won the Seven Years' War (1756-63) but was deep in debt. It taxed the American colonies: the Stamp Act (1765), then duties on tea, glass and paper. Colonists said they had no representatives in Parliament, so taxes were unfair: 'no taxation without representation'. The Boston Massacre (1770) left five colonists dead.
Tea and trouble

The Tea Act (1773) actually made East India Company tea cheaper, even with the tax, but gave the Company a monopoly and accepted Parliament's right to tax. Merchants and radicals objected. Britain answered with harsh 'Coercive Acts' in 1774. Fighting began in April 1775 at Lexington and Concord.
Declaring independence

Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration , adopted on 4 July 1776 (the vote for independence was on 2 July). It said all men are created equal and have the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Jefferson himself held enslaved people.
How they won

George Washington's Continental Army was often short of food and money. The big turn came when the Americans won at Saratoga in 1777, which convinced France to join them in 1778. In 1781 a French fleet and army helped trap General Cornwallis at Yorktown . Britain recognised independence in the Treaty of Paris (1783).
Making a country

The first system, the Articles of Confederation, was weak. A convention at Philadelphia wrote the Constitution in 1787, with separation of powers, a President and a Congress. The Bill of Rights followed (1791). The revolution was a model for others, but it left slavery alone and gave voting rights to few.
Was it a real revolution?

Some say it was a political break, not a social upheaval, since the same rich men kept power. Others say the radical ideas of equality and republican government changed the world. Myth check: 'Tea tax went up.' It did not; the price of legal tea was falling. The argument was about principle and about the Company's power.
Meanwhile in India…

The same company, the same general Lord Cornwallis surrendered to Washington at Yorktown in October 1781. He did not end his career there. He became Governor-General of India in 1786 and fought Tipu Sultan in the Third Anglo-Mysore War, which ended in 1792 with half of Tipu's land lost. In 1793 he introduced the Permanent Settlement of Bengal. The East India Company itself was part of the American story. The Tea Act of 1773, made to rescue the near-bankrupt Company, led to the Boston Tea Party in December that year. A failed empire in America and a growing one in India grew from the same trading corporation.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Taxes without representation sparked the crisis. The Tea Party (1773) was against a Company monopoly. Declaration of Independence was adopted on 4 July 1776. French help won Yorktown (1781). Cornwallis went on to India. Think about it Why did colonists fight over a small tax? Can a revolution claim equality and keep slavery?
The French Revolution
A prison with seven prisoners became the symbol of a revolution

On 14 July 1789, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, a fortress prison. They wanted gunpowder. Inside, there were only seven prisoners. But the Bastille stood for royal power, and its fall shook Europe.
Bankrupt kingdom

France was broke after wars (including helping America). Society had three Estates : clergy, nobles, and everyone else. The Third Estate paid most taxes and had the least say. Bad harvests made bread dear. In May 1789 Louis XVI called the Estates-General to raise money. The Third Estate declared itself a National Assembly and took the Tennis Court Oath (20 June).
Rights and a march

The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August 1789) said men are born free and equal. In October, thousands of Parisian women marched to Versailles and brought the royal family to Paris.
The Terror

In 1793 France was at war with most of Europe and torn by civil war. The Committee of Public Safety, with Robespierre , ruled by fear. The guillotine was used on thousands. Around 17,000 were officially executed; many more died in prisons and revolts, with some estimates of 40,000 deaths. In July 1794 Robespierre himself was guillotined.
Slogans and changes

The revolutionaries abolished feudal privileges, made a new calendar and metric measures, and confiscated Church lands. 'Liberty, equality, fraternity' became the motto. Women did not win the vote. Olympe de Gouges wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman in 1791 and was guillotined in 1793.
After the storm

The chaos ended with a young general taking power in 1799: Napoleon. Historians still argue whether the Revolution brought freedom or just a new strongman. But after 1789, kings everywhere had to worry about what their people might do.
'Let them eat cake'

Myth: Marie Antoinette said it when told that the poor had no bread. Fact: no evidence she said it. A similar line appears in Rousseau's Confessions , written when she was a child, about 'a great princess'. It is propaganda. Also, the Bastille's taking was not about freeing prisoners, and the Revolution did not end the monarchy overnight; it happened over three years.
Meanwhile in India…

Citizen Tipu, and Ambedkar's answer In 1797 French soldiers at Seringapatam planted a Tree of Liberty and founded a Jacobin Club. Tipu Sultan of Mysore, a foe of the British, was enrolled in it as Citizen Tipu. He hoped for French help against the Company. The Revolution's slogans came back in 1949. In the Constituent Assembly, B. R. Ambedkar argued that liberty, equality and fraternity cannot be divorced, or democracy fails. He later said he took the ideas from the Buddha, not from France. The ideals travelled, but Ambedkar added what the French had missed: social democracy, not only political votes.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789. The Declaration of Rights came in August 1789. Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. The Terror lasted 1793-94. Napoleon took power in 1799. Think about it Why do revolutions often turn violent? Who was left out of 'liberty, equality, fraternity'?
Napoleon
The man who crowned himself

On 2 December 1804, in Notre-Dame cathedral, the Pope waited to crown the new emperor of the French. Napoleon took the crown from the Pope's hands and put it on his own head. It was a message: I owe nobody.
The islander

Napoleon Bonaparte was born in 1769 in Ajaccio, Corsica, just after France bought the island. He became an artillery officer. He won fame at Toulon (1793), then in Italy (1796-97). In 1798 he invaded Egypt, partly to threaten British routes to India. He won on land but his fleet was destroyed by Nelson at the Nile. In 1799, he returned and took power in a coup.
Law and glory

As First Consul and then Emperor, Napoleon made the Napoleonic Code (1804): equal rights before the law, protection of property, and religious toleration, but fewer rights for women. It shaped many countries' laws. He won huge victories, like Austerlitz (2 December 1805). Yet Nelson's win at Trafalgar (October 1805) kept Britain safe at sea. He sold Louisiana to the US in 1803.
The rise and fall
In 1812 he invaded Russia with about half a million men. Disease, hunger and the Russian winter destroyed the army; only a small fraction came back. In 1814 he was forced to abdicate.
Hundred Days

He escaped from Elba in 1815 and regained France. At Waterloo (18 June 1815), British and Prussian forces under Wellington and Blucher beat him. He was exiled to St Helena, a lonely island in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.
Legacy

He spread ideas of the Revolution across Europe, breaking old states and awakening nationalism. His wars also killed millions. Afterwards the Congress of Vienna (1814-15) tried to restore the old order and balance of power.
Was Napoleon short?

Myth: he was tiny. Fact: he was about 5 feet 6 or 7 inches in modern measure, average or slightly above for his time. French inches were longer than English ones, and British cartoons drew him as small. His nickname 'le petit caporal' was affectionate. Another point: 'Napoleon complex' is a myth built on that error.
Meanwhile in India…

Napoleon and Tipu Napoleon invaded Egypt in 1798 partly to threaten Britain's road to India. In January 1799 he wrote to Tipu Sultan, offering help against the British. Tipu had already sent envoys to Mauritius in 1798 to ask for French troops, but only a few volunteers came. The letter was too late. On 4 May 1799 Company forces stormed Seringapatam and Tipu died in the fighting. Among the British officers was Arthur Wellesley, brother of the Governor-General, Richard Wellesley. Sixteen years later, as the Duke of Wellington, he beat Napoleon at Waterloo.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Napoleon took power in 1799 and became emperor in 1804. The Napoleonic Code spread legal equality, but not for women. Austerlitz was his greatest victory; Russia (1812) the great disaster. Waterloo ended him in 1815. He wrote to Tipu Sultan in 1798. Think about it Was he the heir of the Revolution or its gravedigger? Why did he fail in Russia?
The Haitian Revolution
The only successful slave revolt that created a country

In the 1780s, the French colony of Saint-Domingue produced more sugar and coffee than any other place on Earth. It was also a hell for about half a million enslaved people. In 1791, they rose. Thirteen years later, they had defeated the armies of France, Spain and Britain, and founded a nation: Haiti.
The richest colony

Saint-Domingue had about 500,000 enslaved people, perhaps 30,000 free people of colour and a similar number of whites. Death rates were so high that planters constantly bought more captives. When the French Revolution began in 1789, the colony fought over who was covered by 'Rights of Man'.
August 1791

In August 1791 a huge uprising began in the north, said to have been launched after a ceremony at Bois Caiman (details are debated). Plantations burned. Leaders emerged, among them Toussaint Louverture , a formerly enslaved man in his late forties who had learned to read.
A leader and a betrayal

In 1794, France's revolutionary government abolished slavery, and Toussaint joined the French side. He ruled the island as governor. Napoleon wanted slavery back. In 1802 he sent a big army. Toussaint was seized by trickery and died in a French prison in April 1803.
Victory

Disease, especially yellow fever, killed many French soldiers. Under Jean-Jacques Dessalines , the rebels won the battle of Vertieres (November 1803). On 1 January 1804 Haiti declared independence, the first Black republic and the first free state in Latin America. The name Haiti was a native Taino word.
The price of freedom

France, and other countries, refused to recognise Haiti. In 1825, France demanded 150 million francs as 'compensation' for lost property, later reduced to 90 million. Haiti borrowed from French banks and paid until 1947. Historians link this debt to Haiti's long poverty. The US only recognised Haiti in 1862.
Is Haiti poor because it is 'cursed'?

Myth: Haiti's troubles come from a curse or a pact. Fact: historians point to concrete causes: the indemnity, trade embargoes, destroyed plantations, later foreign interference and political instability. Another effect: Napoleon lost Saint-Domingue and soon sold Louisiana to the US in 1803. The revolution also terrified slave-owners across the Americas and inspired enslaved people elsewhere.
Meanwhile in India…

Another world, another empire In January 1804 Haiti declared independence under Dessalines, after Toussaint Louverture had died in a French prison in April 1803. In those same months the East India Company was winning the Second Anglo-Maratha War. Arthur Wellesley won at Assaye in September 1803, and General Lake entered Delhi that month. The blind Mughal emperor Shah Alam II became a pensioner under Company protection. Britain's empire was growing in India while enslaved Haitians broke the French sugar empire. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807, even as its Indian territory kept growing, so one empire's ending was another's beginning.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Haiti's revolution began in 1791. Toussaint Louverture led it, then was captured in 1802. Haiti became independent on 1 January 1804. France demanded an indemnity in 1825. The revolution inspired many. Think about it Why did powers refuse to recognise Haiti? Is it fair that the freed paid the former masters?
Bolívar and the Liberation of South America
Five nations from one man's dream

Simón Bolívar led the wars that freed much of Spanish South America. The modern countries of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia all owe part of their story to him. Bolivia takes its name from him. Bolívar was a soldier and a thinker. He wanted a united Latin America. His dream failed, but his ideas still shape how Latin Americans think about freedom and unity.
An oath in Rome

Bolívar was born in Caracas in 1783 to a rich creole family, Spanish-born settlers' children born in America. A popular story says that in 1805, on a hill in Rome, he swore an oath to free his country. The story is often told, but its details are uncertain. He had seen the French Revolution and read Enlightenment writers. He came home determined to end Spanish rule and build a republic.
The war to the death

In 1810 Caracas rebelled, and in 1811 a republic was declared. It collapsed in 1812 after an earthquake and royalist attacks. In 1813 Bolívar issued a decree of "war to the death" against Spaniards who would not join the cause. The war was brutal. Both sides killed prisoners and civilians. Bolívar fled, returned, lost and won again, and he kept fighting until his victories changed the map.
The Jamaica Letter (1815)

Simón Bolívar, Carta de Jamaica (1815) Writing from exile in Jamaica, Bolívar analysed the future of Spanish America. He argued that the region was divided by race, class and geography, and that it would need strong leaders and a new political system. The letter is one of the most important political texts of the age. Its predictions about division proved partly right.
Bolívar's campaigns
His great victories came in 1819 to 1824. By the time he died in 1830, most of Spanish South America had won independence.
Crossing the Andes

In 1819 Bolívar led an army of about two thousand men over the freezing Páramo mountain passes to the plains of New Granada. The march was hard, and many soldiers died of cold and exhaustion. At Boyacá the army surprised the royalists and won a decisive battle. The victory opened the way to Bogotá and made Bolívar the leader of the northern revolution.
Was Bolívar a democrat?

Bolívar is often shown as a democrat who believed in freedom for all. Statues and speeches make him a model of liberal hope. Historians argue that his views were more complex. He admired the British constitution but also wanted strong executive power. His constitution for Bolivia in 1826 gave a president for life, which many saw as a route to dictatorship.
A meeting in Guayaquil

In 1822 Bolívar met José de San Martín, the liberator of Argentina and Chile, at Guayaquil. What they discussed is still debated, but San Martín soon withdrew from public life and left Bolívar to finish the war. The meeting shows how the wars of independence were led by rival generals as well as by armies. Historians still study it to understand the politics of the time.
Gran Colombia breaks apart

Bolívar created Gran Colombia, a union of Venezuela, New Granada and Ecuador, in 1819 to 1822. The union was strained by rivalries between regions and between military leaders. It broke apart in 1830. Bolívar was ill and exhausted when he died in 1830 on the coast of Colombia. He left a legacy of unity that many Latin American leaders tried to recall, but his union did not survive him.
The liberator and the legend

Bolívar became the Liberator in the minds of many people. Monuments, poems and national holidays turned him into a symbol. Later leaders in Venezuela and elsewhere claimed his name for their own causes. Historians argue about how to remember him. Some see a hero who freed a continent. Others see a general who fought a civil war and ruled as a strong man. Both views are part of the story.
Meanwhile in India…

In 1818 the British had ended the Third Anglo-Maratha War and taken much of central India. The East India Company was building an empire of its own on the subcontinent just as Spanish America was breaking away. Britain also gained from Latin American trade. British merchants and volunteers helped the independence wars, and the British Legion fought in Bolívar's army. Two empires, two sets of wars, one global economy.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Bolívar was born in Caracas in 1783. The Jamaica Letter of 1815 analysed Spanish America's future. He won at Boyacá in 1819 and at Ayacucho in 1824. Gran Colombia broke up in 1830. Bolivia is named after him. Think about it Can a continent be united by a single leader's dream? Was Bolívar a democrat, a dictator or both?
The Industrial Revolution
Why did a rainy island change how the whole world works?

Around 1760, one small country began making things with machines and coal instead of hands and muscle. Within a century, the world had factories, railways and slums. That island was Britain. The question is why.
Coal, cotton and steam

Thomas Newcomen built an early steam engine in 1712. James Watt greatly improved it from the 1760s-70s. Spinning machines such as Hargreaves's jenny and Arkwright's water frame (1760s) multiplied output.
Rail and the city

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830, with Stephenson's engines. Manchester grew from a town into a vast 'cotton city'. Factories ran on fixed hours. Time itself got stricter. Trade in raw cotton relied on slave plantations in the American South.
The human price

Workers, including young children, laboured 12-14 hours in noisy mills. Cities lacked clean water and drains, and cholera and typhus spread. Slow reforms followed, such as the Factory Act of 1833, which limited children's hours. In the long run, living standards rose, but for several decades many people were worse off.
Why Britain?

Historians argue. Ideas: coal near the surface, high wages that made machines worth building, an overseas empire for markets and raw materials, secure property rights and a culture of tinkering. Kenneth Pomeranz ( The Great Divergence , 2000) stressed coal and colonies. No single cause is accepted by all.
Were the Luddites against technology?

Myth: Luddites (1811-16) smashed machines because they hated progress. Fact: they were skilled textile workers protesting low pay and loss of their trade. Machine-breaking was a way to bargain. The government sent more troops against them than it had sent to fight Napoleon in some years; the law made machine-breaking punishable by death in 1812.
Meanwhile in India…

The weaver and the mill Before the mills, Bengal's muslin, woven round Dhaka, clothed the rich across the world. British law protected Lancashire: the Calico Acts of 1700 and 1720 limited Indian cloth, and heavy duties kept it out after that. Then Lancashire's machine-made cloth flooded India. India turned from exporter of cloth to supplier of raw cotton. In 1834 the Governor-General William Bentinck is reported to have written that the bones of cotton weavers were bleaching the plains of India. Indians then built their own mills. The first Bombay cotton mill opened in 1854, set up by Cowasji Davar, and Bombay became a mill town.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Britain began industrialising around 1760. Coal, steam and cotton were central. Factories brought both wealth and hardship. Why Britain is debated. India's textile industry suffered; railways came in 1853. Think about it Who gained and who lost in the early factory age? What makes people smash machines?
Japan's Meiji Leap
Four black ships, and a country changed in 15 years

In July 1853, American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry sailed into Edo Bay. They were steam-powered and painted black. Japan, closed to most outsiders for over 200 years, now had to decide. It chose to change faster than any big country had.
The shock
The Tokugawa shogunate looked weak. Young samurai from Satsuma and Choshu rebelled. In 1868 they 'restored' the young Emperor Meiji (aged 15) to power.
Remaking a state

The new government abolished the old feudal domains (1871), ended samurai privileges, created a conscript army (1873), built railways (first line 1872), set up schools and factories. The Iwakura Mission (1871-73) toured the US and Europe to learn. A Constitution came in 1889, with an elected Diet but strong powers for the emperor.
The last samurai
Many samurai lost their income. In 1877 Saigo Takamori , once a hero of the Restoration, led the Satsuma Rebellion. Modern conscript soldiers crushed it. It made clear that the old order was gone.
Joining the imperial club

Japan beat China in the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-95) and took Taiwan. In 1902 it allied with Britain. In 1904-05 it defeated Russia, the first time an Asian power beat a European great power in a modern war. Japan then annexed Korea (1910), becoming an imperial power itself.
Did Japan modernise from nothing?

Myth: a backward country suddenly woke up. Fact: Edo Japan already had big cities (Edo was among the largest in the world), high literacy for the time, banking and trade. Meiji leaders built on that. Also, 'Restoration' was partly a slogan; the real power was held by a small group of ex-samurai officials.
Meanwhile in India…

1905 and Asian pride Japan's win over Russia in 1904–05, sealed at Tsushima in May 1905, thrilled Asia. The young Jawaharlal Nehru later recalled reading the news with delight. An Asian country had beaten a European great power. The same year the British partitioned Bengal, and the Swadeshi movement began. Nationalists pointed to Japan as proof that Asians could modernise on their own terms. Okakura Tenshin, who visited Calcutta in 1901–02 and wrote The Ideals of the East, linked Indian and Japanese thinkers. Rabindranath Tagore visited Japan in 1916. Revolutionaries such as Rash Behari Bose later found refuge in Japan.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Perry arrived in 1853; the Meiji Restoration came in 1868. Reforms: army, schools, railways, constitution (1889). The Satsuma Rebellion (1877) ended samurai power. Japan beat China (1895) and Russia (1905). 1905 inspired Indian nationalists. Think about it Why did Japan change when China resisted? Can rapid modernisation have a dark side?
The Scramble for Africa
In 1870 about a tenth of Africa was ruled by Europeans. By 1914, almost all of it

Imagine losing control of your continent in about 40 years. That is what happened in Africa. Only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent. How? Guns, medicine, railways and a very unusual conference where no African was invited.
The tools
Quinine fought malaria. Steamships went up rivers. The rapid-fire Maxim gun (1884) gave Europeans a huge advantage in battle.
Berlin 1884-85

German chancellor Bismarck hosted a conference in Berlin (November 1884-February 1885). Fourteen states attended, none African. They agreed that to claim land, a power needed 'effective occupation'. It did not draw Africa's map by itself; the carve-up was already under way. But it sparked a rush.
A king's private colony

King Leopold II of Belgium got recognition of the 'Congo Free State' in 1885 as nearly his personal property. Forced rubber collection brought mutilation and killing. Millions died; estimates vary and are debated, with figures like 10 million often cited. After campaigns by E. D. Morel and others, Belgium took it over in 1908.
Resistance

Africans resisted all over. At Adwa on 1 March 1896, Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia crushed an Italian army. The Boer War (1899-1902) pitted Britain against Dutch settlers. In German South West Africa, the Herero and Nama genocide (1904-08) killed tens of thousands. Borders were often straight lines that split peoples and joined rivals. Many modern African conflicts have roots there.
Did Berlin 'divide Africa' in one meeting?

Myth: European leaders sat in Berlin and cut up a map. Fact: the conference dealt with the Congo and the rules for claiming land. Most borders were set later through treaties between powers, and many by field agents. Still, no African ruler had a say, and that is the heart of the injustice.
Meanwhile in India…

Indians in Africa Indians went to Africa as labourers, traders and lawyers. From 1860 indentured workers arrived in Natal to cut sugar cane. The Uganda Railway (1896–1901) was built by about 32,000 Indian labourers, and about 2,500 died. Gandhi arrived in Durban in 1893 as a lawyer for an Indian firm, was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg, and in 1894 founded the Natal Indian Congress. He stayed for twenty-one years. Traders settled along the East African coast, and Zanzibar's Indian merchants financed the Sultan. In 1972 Idi Amin expelled Uganda's Asians, many of them of Indian origin, about 50,000 people.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember By 1914 Europe controlled almost all Africa. The Berlin Conference (1884-85) set the rules, with no Africans present. Leopold's Congo was among the worst. Ethiopia won at Adwa (1896). Indians built the Uganda Railway. Think about it Why did Europe rush in at that moment? What does Adwa teach?
The Opium Wars and China's Century of Humiliation
A war fought over a drug the British grew in India

In 1839, a Chinese official named Lin Zexu seized over 1,000 tonnes of opium from foreign merchants in Canton and destroyed it in trenches with lime and salt water. That act launched a war, and a century of pain China still remembers.
Tea, silver and opium
The East India Company ran an opium monopoly in India and sold the drug at auction in Calcutta to private traders, who shipped it to China.
First Opium War, 1839-42

Britain sent steam-powered warships and sepoys. China's old forts and ships were no match. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) gave Britain Hong Kong, five treaty ports and a large payment, and a later treaty gave extra rights to foreigners. It was the first of the 'unequal treaties'.
Second war and a burned palace

In the Second Opium War (1856-60) Britain and France attacked again. In 1860 they looted and burned the Summer Palace in Beijing. Opium trade was legalised. Meanwhile, the Taiping Rebellion (1850-64) tore China apart from inside. Estimates say over 20 million died.
A 'century of humiliation'

Chinese tradition counts about 1839-1949: lost wars, foreign concessions, and the loss of Taiwan to Japan (1895). Many Chinese leaders today use this story to explain their desire for a strong state. Hong Kong stayed British until 1 July 1997.
Was China just backward and closed?

Myth: China refused to trade, so Britain had to force it open. Fact: China traded widely, through Canton under rules the Qing set. The dispute was over a drug that the government had banned, which merchants smuggled. Historians still argue how much opium harmed China's economy, but the war itself began over this trade.
Meanwhile in India…

Poppy fields and Bombay fortunes Opium was the link between India and China. After Plassey, the Company held a monopoly on opium grown in Bihar and Benares, and auctioned it in Calcutta to private traders who sold it to China. Malwa opium went through Bombay. It was one of the Company's biggest earners. Indian merchants shared in it. The Parsi trader Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy (1783–1859) made a fortune in the China trade, including opium, and his money helped build Bombay's hospitals and schools. Indian soldiers also fought in the First Opium War (1839–42), which ended with Hong Kong ceded to Britain.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Opium paid for British tea. Lin Zexu destroyed opium in 1839. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) gave Hong Kong. The Summer Palace was burned in 1860. India's opium revenue fed the empire. Think about it Is a trade that harms a country ever 'free'? How does a past humiliation shape policy today?
The Taiping Rebellion: China's Deadliest Civil War
A civil war that killed more than the first World War

Between 1850 and 1864 a movement called the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom fought the Qing dynasty across southern and central China. Estimates of the dead run from about 20 million to more than 30 million, which makes it one of the deadliest wars in history. It is less well known than the Opium Wars, but it shaped China's future. The Qing survived, but only by relying on new armies, and the state was weakened for decades.
A failed scholar with a vision

Hong Xiuquan, born in 1814, was a Hakka scholar from Guangdong who failed the civil service exams several times. After a sickness in 1837 he claimed that he had visions of a heavenly father and of Jesus, whom he called his elder brother. He spent years teaching his ideas, which mixed Christian scripture, Chinese tradition and his own revelations. Many poor and dispossessed people in Guangxi were drawn to his message.
The Heavenly Kingdom

In 1851 Hong and his followers declared the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. They attacked and took Nanjing in 1853, which they renamed Tianjing, the Heavenly Capital. They set up a new state with its own calendar, land rules and religious practice. The Taiping banned foot-binding and opium, and they promised land to peasants. These policies appealed to many people, but the movement also became brutal and divided by infighting.
Jonathan Spence and God's Chinese Son

Jonathan Spence, God's Chinese Son (1996) Spence tells the story of Hong Xiuquan with great skill. He shows how Hong's visions, his conflicts with his followers and his failures shaped the rebellion. The book is a good starting point, though it depends on the surviving Taiping texts, which are partial and shaped by propaganda.
The rebellion in key dates
The movement lasted about fourteen years. In that time it held a large region, but the Qing fought back and regained control.
Civil war and the leadership crisis

In 1856 a violent power struggle broke out among the Taiping leaders. Thousands were killed, and the movement lost its best commanders. Hong stayed isolated in Nanjing, and his authority was no longer secure. The crisis weakened the Taiping at the very moment that the Qing began to organise new armies. The rebels never fully recovered the momentum of their early years.
The new Qing armies

The Qing relied on local militias led by scholars such as Zeng Guofan. He raised the Xiang Army from his home province of Hunan. The state also hired foreign soldiers, including the Ever Victorious Army led by Frederick Townsend Ward and later Charles Gordon. These armies fought the Taiping for years. Zeng Guofan's success showed that the Qing could still produce talented generals, but it also gave local leaders more power.
Was Hong a Christian prophet?

Hong is often described in the West as a Chinese Christian who tried to bring Christianity to China. This picture made the rebellion seem like a religious crusade. Historians argue that Hong's religion was heavily reshaped by his visions and his own reading of the Bible. Western missionaries who met him were often shocked by his views. His movement was religious, but it was also political and social.
Hong's death and the fall of Nanjing

Hong Xiuquan died in June 1864, shortly before the Qing forces broke into Nanjing. Accounts say he died of illness or by taking poison. The city was taken in July 1864 and was heavily destroyed. The fall of Nanjing ended the Taiping state. The killings and destruction in the capital and nearby towns were huge, and they added to the death toll of the war.
A war that shaped modern China

The Taiping Rebellion left deep scars. Large areas of the Yangtze valley were devastated, and population and farming took decades to recover. The war also showed how fragile the Qing was, and it weakened the dynasty in the decades that followed. Chinese historians have often seen the Taiping as a precursor to the revolution of the 1900s. Historians argue about how far the movement really anticipated modern ideas.
Meanwhile in India…

The Taiping war overlapped with the 1857 revolt in India. The British had been fighting the Second Opium War in China, and troops that were headed to China were diverted to India when the revolt broke out. Lord Elgin, the British envoy in China, saw his forces redirected to the subcontinent. Two great revolts and two imperial wars were running at once, with British power stretched across Asia.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Hong Xiuquan led the Taiping movement from 1851. Nanjing was taken in 1853 and retaken by the Qing in 1864. Zeng Guofan built a new army in Hunan. The war killed millions and weakened the Qing. Western missionaries rejected Hong's teachings. Think about it Why did the Qing need foreign help to beat a rebellion? Was the Taiping a religious movement, a social revolt or a political one?
Peter the Great and the Window to Europe
A tsar who wanted Europe

Peter the Great ruled Russia from 1682 and alone from 1696 to 1725. He wanted Russia to be a European power. He fought wars, built a new capital, and changed the way Russia was governed, taxed and educated. Peter's reign set the pattern of Russian history for centuries. Historians still argue about whether he modernised Russia or merely copied the West.
A young tsar and a palace revolt

Peter was born in 1672. He became joint tsar at ten with his half-brother Ivan, after a palace uprising. His half-sister Sophia ruled as regent until a new revolt in 1689 forced her out. As a youth, Peter was fascinated by ships, foreign engineering and military drill. He built a small fleet on Lake Pleshcheyevo and a set of model soldiers, and he learned the basics of shipbuilding.
The Great Embassy, 1697

In 1697 Peter travelled through Europe with a large embassy. He went incognito under the name Peter Mikhailov, and he worked in the Dutch shipyards and the English dockyards. He also visited Prussia. The trip brought back new ideas about ships, medicine, printing and government. Peter also brought foreign craftsmen and officers to Russia, and he began to push his nobles to adopt Western dress and manners.
The Table of Ranks (1722)

Table of Ranks Peter's Table of Ranks set out 14 grades for civil and military service. Anyone who reached a certain grade gained noble status, whatever his birth. Service to the state became the path to power. The reform was a major break with older ideas of birth and privilege, though nobles still kept most of their advantages.
Peter's reign in key dates
Peter's reign combined war, reform and building. It turned Russia into a major European state.
The Great Northern War

In 1700 Russia joined a coalition against Sweden. The war lasted until 1721. At first the Swedes won, but at Poltava in 1709 Peter's army defeated Charles XII. The victory gave Russia control of the Baltic coast. Peter's army was trained on European lines, with a new officer corps and better artillery. The war cost Russia huge sums, and it was paid for with taxes, conscription and forced labour.
St Petersburg: a window to Europe

In 1703 Peter founded St Petersburg on the marshy delta of the Neva river. Thousands of serfs died building it. The city became the new capital in 1712 and a model of European planning, with canals, palaces and straight avenues. Peter called it his "window to Europe". The city was a bold symbol of change, and historians still debate whether the price was worth paying.
Did Peter personally cut off beards?

A popular image shows Peter the Great with scissors, cutting the beards of his nobles. The picture is vivid and easy to remember. Peter did impose a beard tax and ordered nobles to shave, and many men resisted. Historians argue about how far Peter personally enforced these rules. The beard tax was real, but the image of Peter as a single barber is exaggerated.
Was it modernisation or westernisation?

Historians argue about what Peter's reforms meant. Some say he modernised Russia by making its army, navy, administration and science more effective. Others say he westernised a society that was not ready, and that the reforms created a split between elites and peasants. The debate is still alive, because Russians still argue about how Russia should relate to Europe. Peter remains a central figure in that argument.
A tsar who was also a worker

Peter took a practical interest in trades. He learned carpentry and shipbuilding, and he worked as a shipwright in the Netherlands. He was very tall, around two metres, and he had a fierce temper. His personal energy made him a figure of legend. He also drove his subjects hard, and many did not share his enthusiasm for change.
Meanwhile in India…

When Peter founded St Petersburg in 1703, the Mughal empire was still ruling India under Aurangzeb, who died in 1707. The decades after his death brought revolts by Marathas, Sikhs and regional governors. In 1739 Nadir Shah of Persia sacked Delhi and took the Peacock Throne. Russia was rising, and India was splitting into rival states. The two empires faced very different futures.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Peter ruled alone from 1696. His Great Embassy to Europe ran from 1697 to 1698. He founded St Petersburg in 1703. The Table of Ranks of 1722 linked noble status to state service. Russia became an empire in 1721. Think about it Can a state modernise without copying others? Was St Petersburg worth the human cost of building it?
The First World War
A wrong turn in Sarajevo lit a fuse across the world

On 28 June 1914, the Austrian heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, was driving through Sarajevo. His car stalled after an earlier bomb attempt failed. A 19-year-old named Gavrilo Princip was standing nearby. He shot the Archduke and his wife. Within six weeks, Europe was at war.
The fuse
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia. Alliances pulled in Russia, Germany, France and Britain. Germany's plan was to knock out France fast. It failed, and the armies dug in.
The trenches

From late 1914 the Western Front was a line of trenches from the sea to Switzerland. Machine guns made charging deadly. On 1 July 1916, the first day of the Somme, Britain suffered about 57,000 casualties, with about 19,000 killed. New horrors: poison gas (used at Ypres in 1915), tanks (1916), aircraft and submarines.
A truce and a long war

At Christmas 1914, soldiers on parts of the front stopped firing and swapped gifts. It was short-lived and not general. In 1917 the US joined after German submarine attacks, while Russia, torn by revolution, left the war. Germany asked for an armistice, which began on 11 November 1918 .
The cost

Roughly 9-10 million soldiers died, plus millions of civilians. Four empires fell: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. The Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany and imposed reparations. The 1918-19 influenza pandemic, helped by troop movements, killed many more.
Whose fault was it?

After the war, Germany was blamed. In 1961 Fritz Fischer argued Germany pushed for war. In 2012 Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers argued all powers stumbled into it. A famous myth: soldiers were 'lions led by donkeys'. Historians now say that image is too simple, since commanders learned and tactics improved.
Meanwhile in India…

The forgotten army More than 1.3 million Indians served overseas in the war, and about 74,000 died. They fought in France, at Neuve Chapelle in 1915, and in Mesopotamia, East Africa and Gallipoli. Khudadad Khan won the first Victoria Cross for an Indian soldier in October 1914. Indians hoped that service would bring self-rule. In 1917 the British promised responsible government in stages. The Rowlatt Acts of 1919 and the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on 13 April 1919 broke that hope. India Gate in Delhi, finished in 1931, is a memorial to these soldiers.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The war began after Sarajevo in 1914. Trench warfare killed millions. Ended on 11 November 1918. Four empires collapsed. Indians served in large numbers. Think about it Why did alliances make a local crisis global? What did India get for its sacrifice?
The Russian Revolution
A sealed train, a tsar's abdication and a revolution in a week

In April 1917, a train carrying Lenin from exile in Switzerland rolled across Germany toward Russia. Germany let it pass, hoping he would weaken Russia's war effort. It worked, beyond what anyone expected.
The tsar falls

Russia in 1917 was exhausted by war, with food shortages. In Petrograd, strikes and women's marches on 8 March (23 February in the old calendar) grew into revolt. Soldiers joined the crowds. Nicholas II abdicated. The Romanov dynasty, 300 years old, was over. A Provisional Government took charge, but kept fighting the war.
Peace, land, bread
Lenin's Bolsheviks promised 'Peace, land and bread'. On 25 October (7 November, new calendar), they took over the capital and government buildings with little fighting.
Civil war

Reds (Bolsheviks) fought Whites (various opponents), with foreign intervention. The war lasted to 1922. Millions died from fighting, famine and disease. The Bolsheviks created the secret police, the Cheka. The tsar and his family were shot in July 1918 at Yekaterinburg.
A new state

In 1922 the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was founded. After Lenin died in 1924, Stalin beat Trotsky in the struggle for power. The state took over industry and farms and ruled by terror in the 1930s. The Revolution inspired communists and anticolonial movements across the world.
Did the Bolsheviks storm the Winter Palace in a huge battle?

Myth: thousands charged the Palace in a bloody fight. Fact: the real seizure was fairly quiet, with few casualties. The famous images come from Eisenstein's 1928 film October and later propaganda. Also: the date. Russia used the Julian calendar until 1918, so the 'October' revolution is on 7 November in our calendar.
Meanwhile in India…

Red ideas travel The revolution in Russia gave Indian radicals a new model. M. N. Roy, at the Comintern's Second Congress in 1920, argued that colonial lands mattered to world revolution, and he helped form an Indian communist group at Tashkent that year. The Communist Party of India held its first conference at Kanpur in December 1925. The British answered with the Kanpur (1924) and Meerut (1929) conspiracy cases. Nehru visited Moscow in November 1927. Bhagat Singh read Lenin. The Soviet idea of planning later shaped India's own five-year plans, which began in 1951.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The tsar fell in February 1917. The Bolsheviks took power in October 1917. A civil war lasted to 1922. The USSR was created in 1922. India's thinkers were inspired. Think about it Why did the Provisional Government fail? Is a revolution made by leaders, or by crowds?
The Great Depression
The crash did not cause it alone, but it lit the match

On Tuesday 29 October 1929, panicked investors dumped 16 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange. Prices crashed. Within four years, a quarter of American workers had no job, and the whole world was in trouble.
Boom to bust
Thousands of US banks failed in the early 1930s, and there was no deposit insurance. World trade shrank by about two thirds.
Wrong medicine

Governments cut spending and raised tariffs. The US Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) set high import taxes, and other countries retaliated. Staying on the gold standard forced many countries into deflation. By 1933 US unemployment was about 25 percent, and in Germany about 6 million were jobless.
The New Deal and Keynes

In 1933 Franklin D. Roosevelt took office and began the New Deal : bank rescue, public works, Social Security (1935). John Maynard Keynes's General Theory (1936) argued that governments should spend to revive demand in a slump. Historians still argue how much the New Deal did; the real recovery came with war spending.
Politics turns ugly

Hardship fed anger. In Germany the Nazis rose from a small party to the largest in 1932. In Japan, the military gained power. The Depression did not make World War II certain, but it made it much likelier.
Did stockbrokers jump from windows?

Myth: after the crash, ruined brokers leapt from skyscrapers by the dozen. Fact: it makes a dramatic story, but records show very few suicides in those weeks. Also, the crash itself did not cause the Depression: weak banks, debt and bad policy turned a crash into a catastrophe.
Meanwhile in India…

Farmers and gold The Depression hit India's farmers hard. Crop prices fell by about half after 1929 while rents, taxes and debts stayed the same. Peasant anger fed the Civil Disobedience Movement, which began with Gandhi's Salt March in March 1930. Britain left the gold standard in September 1931, but the rupee stayed fixed to the pound. Poor families sold gold ornaments to survive, and India's gold flowed out in what was called distress gold. The gold sold off helped Britain pay its own debts. In March 1931 Gandhi and Viceroy Irwin signed a pact, with the Depression biting at home.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The 1929 crash began the slump. Bank failures and falling trade made it a global depression. Wrong policies worsened it. The New Deal and Keynes changed economic thinking. Hardship helped extremists rise. Think about it Should governments spend more in a slump? Why did the Depression hit farmers in India?
Fascism and Nazism
How a dictator was handed power by people who thought they could control him

On 30 January 1933, the German president Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler as chancellor. Conservative politicians thought they could use him and keep him in check. Within 18 months he had no checks left.
Mussolini goes first

Fascism began in Italy. Mussolini , once a socialist, led his Blackshirts in the 'March on Rome' (October 1922). The king asked him to form a government. By 1925 he had made himself dictator. Fascists glorified the nation, the leader and violence, and hated democracy, liberals and socialists.
Hitler's rise

After a failed coup in 1923, Hitler turned to elections. The Nazis won 37 percent in July 1932, their best free result. After the Reichstag fire (February 1933) and the Enabling Act (March 1933), Germany became a one-party dictatorship.
Racism as state policy

The Nazis claimed 'Aryans' were a master race. They stripped Jews of citizenship and rights with the Nuremberg Laws (1935). On 9-10 November 1938 came Kristallnacht , when synagogues and Jewish shops were smashed and about 30,000 Jewish men arrested. Hitler's regime also persecuted Roma, disabled people, homosexuals and political opponents.
Why did it work?

Reasons historians give: economic misery, anger over Versailles, fear of communism, weak democratic habits, clever propaganda by Joseph Goebbels, and violence by the SA. The Nazi state also gave many Germans jobs and national pride. But the same state was a machine of terror, with the Gestapo, camps and no free press.
Was Hitler elected dictator?

Myth: Germans voted him in as dictator. Fact: the Nazis never won a majority in a free election. In November 1932 their share fell to about 33 percent. Hindenburg and conservative politicians appointed Hitler chancellor. He then used emergency powers to destroy democracy. It shows how fragile democracy can be when elites bargain with extremists.
Meanwhile in India…

Bose, Gandhi and Nehru Indian leaders saw fascism differently. Nehru refused to meet Mussolini in 1936 and in 1938 visited Republican Spain. Gandhi wrote to Hitler in July 1939 and again in December 1940, addressing him as friend, to plead for peace. The letters did not reach him or did not matter. Subhas Chandra Bose, Congress president in 1938–39, left Congress after clashing with Gandhi and formed the Forward Bloc. In 1941 he escaped to Germany, met Hitler in 1942, and sought Axis help to free India. In 1943 he went on to Japan and Singapore to lead the Indian National Army.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Mussolini took power in 1922. Hitler was appointed in January 1933. The Enabling Act ended democracy. Nuremberg Laws and Kristallnacht targeted Jews. Bose, Gandhi and Nehru reacted differently. Think about it How can democracies protect themselves? Why did people support or tolerate the regime?
The Second World War
The deadliest war in history, in five dates

On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Britain and France declared war two days later. Over six years, the war killed an estimated 70-85 million people, most of them civilians. Here is the story in the fewest possible steps.
Blitzkrieg and Britain alone
Germany's fast attack, Blitzkrieg , conquered Poland and then France in six weeks (1940). Britain held out in the Battle of Britain, with Churchill's leadership.
The East and the Pacific

In June 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union. On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and the US entered the war. The Soviets beat Germany at Stalingrad (1942-43). The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people. In June 1944 Allied forces landed in Normandy ( D-Day , 6 June). Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945.
The bomb

The US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August). Japan announced surrender on 15 August; the formal signing was on 2 September. Historians still argue about whether the bombs were needed, or whether the Soviet entry into the war was decisive.
The cost and the aftermath

Cities lay in ruins, and tens of millions were displaced. The war gave birth to the United Nations (1945), the Nuremberg trials, and a world with two superpowers, the US and USSR. It also made colonial empires harder to hold.
Did the war start only in Europe in 1939?

Myth: WWII started with Poland. Fact: in Asia, Japan invaded China in 1937 (or Manchuria in 1931), so for China the war began earlier. Also, Allied victory was not only the work of the US and Britain: the Soviet Union and China bore enormous losses.
Meanwhile in India…

An army, a famine and a movement The Indian Army grew to over 2.5 million, the largest volunteer force in the war. Its men fought in North Africa, Italy, Burma and Kohima-Imphal in 1944. At home, Gandhi launched Quit India on 8 August 1942 and the leaders were jailed. In 1943, Bengal's famine killed some two to three million. Bose's INA fought alongside Japan. After the war, the British put INA officers on trial at the Red Fort in 1945–46. Crowds protested, and in February 1946 Royal Indian Navy sailors mutinied. Britain saw that it could no longer rely on India's army.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember WWII began in 1939 (earlier in Asia). Germany attacked the USSR in 1941; Pearl Harbor drew in the US. D-Day 1944; Germany surrendered May 1945. Atomic bombs preceded Japan's surrender in August 1945. India contributed troops and suffered a famine. Think about it Was the bombing of cities justified? How did the war speed up decolonisation?
The Holocaust
The murder of six million, planned like paperwork

This lesson is heavy. We tell it plainly because it must be remembered precisely. Between 1933 and 1945, Nazi Germany and its collaborators persecuted Jews and then murdered about six million of them, two thirds of Europe's Jewish population.
Step by step
The process began with exclusion, then ghettos, then killing. After the invasion of the USSR in 1941, mobile units called Einsatzgruppen shot over a million Jews, mostly in pits.
The 'Final Solution'

At the Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942), officials coordinated the plan to murder all European Jews. Death camps such as Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec and Auschwitz-Birkenau used gas chambers. About 1.1 million people were murdered at Auschwitz, around 1 million of them Jews. It needed trains, clerks, police and the silence of many.
Others, and resistance

The Nazis also murdered Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, Poles and political prisoners. Jews resisted too, in ghetto uprisings: the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (April-May 1943) was the largest. Some non-Jews risked their lives to hide Jews. Israel's Yad Vashem honours them as 'Righteous Among the Nations'.
Justice and memory

After the war, the Nuremberg trials (1945-46) tried leading Nazis. Raphael Lemkin, a Polish-Jewish lawyer, coined the word genocide in 1944. The UN adopted the Genocide Convention in 1948. Holocaust Remembrance Day is observed on 27 January, the day Auschwitz was liberated in 1945.
'The Germans didn't know' and 'Jews didn't fight back'

Myth 1: ordinary Germans did not know. Fact: many people saw deportations and knew of killings; how much they knew of the camps is debated, but the persecution was public. Myth 2: Jews went passively. Fact: there was armed resistance in many ghettos and camps, as well as vast spiritual and hidden resistance.
Meanwhile in India…

The Good Maharaja Digvijaysinhji, the Jam Sahib of Nawanagar, ruled a small Gujarat state. In 1942 Polish children who had been taken to Soviet camps and then reached Iran came to India, and he took them into a camp at Balachadi near Jamnagar. An estimated 1,000 children were sheltered there until 1946. Poland later honoured him, and in 2012 a Warsaw square was named after the Good Maharaja. The children grew up speaking Polish in a Gujarati village, and many remembered it as a home. India's own Jews, the Cochin Jews and Bene Israel, had lived for centuries without persecution.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember About six million Jews were murdered. The process moved from exclusion to killing. Wannsee coordinated it in January 1942. Others were murdered too; resistance existed. Genocide became a legal term. Think about it Why must we remember specifics? What allows ordinary people to take part in atrocities?
Stalingrad: The Turning Point
The city that turned the war

Stalingrad, on the Volga river, was the site of the bloodiest battle of the Second World War in Europe. From August 1942 to February 1943 German and Soviet armies fought street by street. The battle is often seen as the turning point of the war on the Eastern Front. Its scale, its suffering and its myths are still debated.
Hitler's city on the Volga

In the summer of 1942 the German Sixth Army under General Friedrich Paulus pushed toward Stalingrad, a city named after Stalin. Hitler wanted the city for its symbol and its control of the river. The city was reduced to ruins by bombing. Soviet soldiers and civilians fought on in the rubble, and the Germans became trapped in the streets.
Encirclement

In November 1942 the Red Army launched Operation Uranus. Soviet forces attacked the weak Romanian and Italian armies on the flanks of the German forces and then closed a ring around Stalingrad. Some 250,000 German and allied troops were trapped in the pocket. Hitler forbade a breakout, and he promised that an airlift would supply the army. The airlift failed.
Vasily Grossman's war reporting

Vasily Grossman (1905–1964) A Soviet writer and war correspondent, Grossman reported from Stalingrad and later wrote the novel Life and Fate . His letters and articles show the cold, the rubble and the crowded dugouts. His work is a vivid source, though it was shaped by the needs of Soviet propaganda and by his own experience.
The battle in key dates
The campaign lasted about five months. After the surrender, most of the surviving German prisoners were marched into captivity.
Life in the ruins

Soldiers fought in cellars, factories and sewers. Some of the most famous fighting was at the Red October steel works and the Barrikady gun factory, where workers kept producing weapons under fire. Civilians stayed in the ruins too, sheltering in cellars and tunnels. Estimates of civilian and military deaths run to more than a million in the battle and the surrounding campaign.
The sniper duel that never happened?

A famous story says that the Soviet sniper Vasily Zaitsev killed hundreds of Germans and fought a deadly duel with a German sniper named Major König. The story was turned into a popular film in 2001. Historians such as Antony Beevor doubt the duel ever took place. The story was partly propaganda, built to inspire Soviet soldiers. Zaitsev was a real sniper, but the duel is probably a legend. Historians argue about how many of the famous Soviet stories were made up.
The surrender

On 31 January 1943 Paulus surrendered, having been made a field marshal the day before. Hitler had hoped that no German field marshal would be taken alive. The last pockets surrendered in early February. About 90,000 German soldiers were taken prisoner. Few of them survived captivity, and only a small fraction returned home after the war.
Why it mattered

Stalingrad destroyed the Sixth Army and cost Germany a large part of its best troops. The Soviets gained the initiative on the Eastern Front, and their advance toward Berlin began. Historians argue about how far Stalingrad was the turning point. Some say the Soviets had already started to recover, and that the battles at Kursk and elsewhere mattered as much. Still, the shock was enormous.
The city after the war

Stalingrad was rebuilt after the war and renamed Volgograd in 1961. The ruins of the old city were partly left as a memorial. The Mamayev Kurgan hill memorial is among the largest war memorials in the world. The name changes show how the city became a symbol. Russians still debate the battle and its meaning, and museums and monuments keep its memory alive.
A battle in memory

The battle became a symbol of Soviet endurance and sacrifice. Novels, films and textbooks celebrated it. Western accounts focused on the German defeat and the tragedy of the Sixth Army. Each memory has its own angle. The most useful history is the one that holds both the heroism and the cruelty of the battle together.
Meanwhile in India…

In 1943, while Stalingrad was being fought, the Bengal famine killed an estimated two to three million people in India. Wartime shipping, rice prices and the movement of food played a role. The economist Amartya Sen later argued that the famine was less about the lack of food than about who could get it. Historians still argue about the blame. Two great wartime disasters ran side by side on opposite sides of the world.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The battle of Stalingrad ran from August 1942 to February 1943. The Soviets encircled the Sixth Army in November 1942. Paulus surrendered on 31 January 1943. About 90,000 German soldiers were captured. The Zaitsev duel is probably a legend. Think about it Did Stalingrad turn the war, or was it one step in a longer turn? How do nations build myths around their wars?
The Cold War and the Bomb
Thirteen days when the world nearly ended

In October 1962, the US found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, 150 km from Florida. For 13 days the two superpowers stared at each other. That was the Cold War: no direct war between the US and USSR, but constant fear, spies, proxy wars and enough bombs to wreck the planet.
How it started
The wartime allies split over Eastern Europe. The US offered the Truman Doctrine (1947) and Marshall Plan to resist communism. The USSR built a bloc of satellite states.
Two camps
The superpowers never fought directly. They fought through others: Korea (1950-53), Vietnam, Afghanistan. The doctrine of Mutual Assured Destruction held that a nuclear attack would destroy both.
Saved by individuals

During the Cuban crisis a Soviet submarine officer, Vasili Arkhipov , reportedly refused to agree to fire a nuclear torpedo. In 1983 Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov judged a missile alarm to be false and did not report it as an attack. Historians agree these were real near-misses, though details are debated.
Ending the crisis

Kennedy and Khrushchev agreed that the USSR would remove missiles from Cuba and the US would pledge not to invade. A secret part of the deal: the US would withdraw missiles from Turkey later. A hotline between Washington and Moscow was set up in 1963.
Did the US simply win by staring down the Soviets?

Myth: Kennedy forced a Soviet retreat with no concessions. Fact: the secret Turkey deal was kept hidden for years. Both sides compromised. Also, 'Cold' is misleading: millions died in proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Angola and elsewhere.
Meanwhile in India…

Neither camp India chose to stay out of both blocs. Nehru said the country would not join either side. In 1954 India and China signed the Panchsheel principles. In 1955 Nehru was at Bandung, and in 1961 he was one of the founders of the Non-Aligned Movement at Belgrade, with Tito and Nasser. Non-alignment meant taking help from all sides. The Soviet Union helped build the Bhilai steel plant (1955), and American wheat under the PL-480 scheme fed Indians in the 1950s and 1960s. In 1971 India signed a treaty with the Soviet Union during the Bangladesh crisis, a sign that neutrality had limits.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Cold War began after 1945. NATO (1949) faced the Warsaw Pact (1955). Wars were fought by proxy. Cuba 1962 was the closest call. India led non-alignment. Think about it Is nuclear deterrence a peace or a gamble? Was non-alignment neutral or just independent?
Decolonisation: Empires End
In 1945 empires ruled a third of humanity. By 1975 they were gone

When the UN was founded in 1945, it had 51 members. Today it has 193. Almost all the extra countries are former colonies. In about thirty years, one of the biggest political changes in human history took place.
The great shift
World War II had drained Britain and France. The US and USSR both pushed against old empires. Colonised people had also fought in the war and wanted freedom.
Different roads

India's freedom came via mass non-violent movements and then talks. Vietnam beat France at Dien Bien Phu (1954) after a long war. In Algeria, a brutal war (1954-62) ended French rule.
