Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah won independence in 1957 through strikes and elections. Britain used force against the Mau Mau in Kenya, with serious abuses.
Suez, 1956

Britain and France, with Israel, attacked Egypt to retake the Suez Canal. The US and USSR forced them to withdraw. It showed the old powers were no longer in charge. In 1960 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 1514, declaring colonialism must end.
Unfinished business

New states inherited borders that cut across peoples. Many faced coups, civil wars and poverty. Portugal held its colonies until 1974-75. Some historians call the continuing economic influence of ex-rulers 'neocolonialism' (a term of Nkrumah's, 1965).
Was decolonisation always peaceful?

Myth: empires handed power over politely. Fact: there were many wars: Algeria, Vietnam, Kenya, Angola, Indonesia. Even India's independence came with Partition, in which perhaps one to two million died (estimates vary) and about 15 million were displaced.
Meanwhile in India…

A tryst with destiny At midnight on 14–15 August 1947 India became free, and Nehru gave his speech, Tryst with Destiny. Pakistan came into being a day earlier. India's freedom was the first big blow to the European empires in Asia. Burma left the Empire in January 1948, Ceylon in February 1948 and Indonesia won independence in 1949. Nehru had hosted the Asian Relations Conference in Delhi in March 1947, and India led demands at the UN against colonial rule. Freedom came with Partition, which killed hundreds of thousands of people and uprooted some 15 million. Decolonisation was never only a celebration.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The UN grew from 51 to far more members. Roads to freedom differed. Suez (1956) showed old powers' decline. Many new states faced hard borders. India helped lead the Afro-Asian cause. Think about it Why did colonial powers lose will? Do old borders cause today's conflicts?
Mao's China
The man who unified China, then lost track of how many he lost

On 1 October 1949, standing on Tiananmen, Mao Zedong announced the People's Republic of China. 'China has stood up,' he said, according to the common account. He would rule for 27 years. The results were mixed and often terrible.
Victory
The Communists won the civil war against the Nationalists (Kuomintang), who fled to Taiwan. Land reform took land from landlords, and many were killed. China fought the US in Korea.
The Great Leap Forward

In 1958 Mao tried to leap into industry with village steel furnaces and giant communes. Bad planning, false harvest reports and forced grain collection caused a famine. Estimates of deaths run from about 15 to 45 million, commonly about 30 million. The exact number is debated. Mao stepped back, but kept power.
Cultural Revolution

In 1966 Mao urged young Red Guards to attack 'bourgeois' elements. Teachers, officials and intellectuals were beaten and humiliated. Schools closed. The Little Red Book of his quotes was waved by millions. The army had to restore order, and the chaos ended with Mao's death on 9 September 1976.
Afterwards

Deng Xiaoping took over and launched reform and opening in 1978. The Communist Party itself, in 1981, judged Mao as 70 percent right and 30 percent wrong, though that figure is a Party formula. Mao's portrait still hangs on Tiananmen.
Great leader or great disaster?

Supporters credit Mao with ending foreign domination, raising literacy and life expectancy. Critics (such as Frank Dikötter) stress the famine and terror. Both can be true. Estimates of famine deaths vary with the method. A myth check: the 'Four Pests' campaign, including killing sparrows, did upset the ecosystem and probably worsened crop losses, but it was not the main cause of famine.
Meanwhile in India…

Hindi-Chini and a border war In the 1950s Indian crowds shouted Hindi-Chini bhai bhai. India signed the Panchsheel agreement with China in 1954 and recognised its control of Tibet. In 1959 the Dalai Lama fled to India after a Tibetan revolt. Trust collapsed over the border. China built a road through Aksai Chin, and India held to the McMahon Line in the east. On 20 October 1962 China attacked in both sectors, then declared a ceasefire on 21 November and withdrew in the east. The defeat shocked India, shook Nehru, who died in 1964, and led to a major military build-up and a change in how India saw its giant neighbour.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The PRC was founded on 1 October 1949. The Great Leap Forward (1958-62) caused famine. The Cultural Revolution lasted 1966-76. Deng began reform in 1978. The 1962 war shaped India-China ties. Think about it Can a leader's aims justify huge costs? How did the 1962 war change India?
The Space Race
A beeping ball the size of a beach ball scared America

On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 , a 58-cm metal sphere. It beeped as it circled Earth. People with radios could hear it. Americans feared Soviet rockets could now carry bombs. The race to space had begun.
Soviet firsts
The Soviets sent the dog Laika (November 1957) and then Yuri Gagarin , who orbited Earth for 108 minutes on 12 April 1961.
Kennedy's bet

Weeks later, President Kennedy told Congress the US would land a man on the Moon before the decade ended. In 1962 he said 'we choose to go to the Moon'. Apollo cost the equivalent of well over a hundred billion modern dollars. In 1967 three astronauts died in the Apollo 1 fire.
20 July 1969

Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed Apollo 11's lander on the Moon, while Michael Collins orbited above. Armstrong stepped out first. About 600 million people watched on TV. Six Apollo missions landed 12 men by 1972. The Soviet Moon rocket, the N1, exploded repeatedly and never worked.
From rivals to partners
In 1975, an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz docked in orbit. Later, the two nations built the International Space Station (from 1998). Today, private firms and many countries also launch rockets.
Was the Moon landing faked? Did NASA spend millions on a pen?

Myth 1: it was faked. Fact: evidence includes 382 kg of Moon rock, reflectors left on the surface that scientists still use, and independent tracking by other countries. Myth 2: NASA built a space pen while the Soviets used a pencil. In fact, pencils were used by both, and the Fisher pen was developed privately.
Meanwhile in India…

From a bicycle to Mars India's space programme began small. On 21 November 1963 the first rocket was launched from Thumba in Kerala, a church was the control room, and parts were carried by bicycle and bullock cart. Vikram Sarabhai led the effort. India launched Aryabhata, its first satellite, in 1975 on a Soviet rocket. In 1984 Rakesh Sharma flew on a Soviet Soyuz. Chandrayaan-1 (2008) helped find water on the Moon. In September 2014 Mangalyaan entered Mars orbit on its first attempt, at a cost lower than many film budgets. In August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole, a first for any country.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Sputnik (1957) started the race. Gagarin was first in space (1961). Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969. The rivals later cooperated. India went from a bicycle to Mars. Think about it Was the race worth it? What can India's low-cost model teach?
1989: The Wall Falls
A press conference mistake ended a divided Europe

On the evening of 9 November 1989, East German official Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules. Asked when they took effect, he shuffled his notes and said, 'immediately, without delay'. He had not been told it was meant for the next day. Crowds rushed to the Berlin Wall. Guards, overwhelmed, opened the gates.
The cracks appear
In Poland, the union Solidarity won the June 1989 elections. In summer Hungary opened its border with Austria, and thousands of East Germans left through it.
Gorbachev lets go

Mikhail Gorbachev , Soviet leader from 1985, began glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring). Crucially, he refused to use Soviet tanks to prop up Eastern European regimes, unlike in 1956 and 1968. So one by one, the regimes fell, mostly peacefully: the 'Velvet Revolution' in Czechoslovakia, and bloody in Romania, where Ceausescu was shot on 25 December.
Not everywhere
In China, the 1989 Tiananmen protests were crushed on 4 June. Beijing's leaders chose force and kept power. It shows the outcome was not inevitable. Germany reunified on 3 October 1990.
The Soviet end

Weakened by economics and nationalism, the USSR itself broke up. In August 1991 hardliners attempted a coup and failed. Boris Yeltsin rose. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned and the USSR dissolved into 15 states.
Who ended the Cold War?

Some credit Reagan's pressure and his 1987 call 'Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall'. Others credit Gorbachev's choices, the weak Soviet economy, or ordinary people in the streets. Most historians say many causes combined. Myth check: the Wall did not fall in one night by hand; much of it was pulled down over the following months and years.
Meanwhile in India…

1991: India's own turning point The fall of the Soviet bloc hit India, which had traded heavily with Moscow. In 1991 the country was nearly out of dollars, with reserves for only about three weeks of imports. The Gulf War had raised oil prices and cut remittances. P. V. Narasimha Rao's government, with Manmohan Singh as finance minister, devalued the rupee in July 1991 and pledged gold to raise cash. It ended much of the licence raj, cut import duties and opened the economy to foreign investment. The Soviet collapse in December 1991 ended the old trade, so India turned to the world market. It began the growth that followed.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Eastern Europe's regimes fell in 1989. Gorbachev refused to use force. The Wall opened on 9 November 1989. Germany reunified in 1990; the USSR ended in 1991. India liberalised in 1991. Think about it Was it inevitable or lucky? Why did China differ?
The Korean War: The Forgotten War
A war that never officially ended

The Korean War was fought from June 1950 to July 1953. It ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty, so the two Koreas are still technically at war. Its cost in lives was enormous, and its shape still defines East Asia. The war showed how the Cold War could turn hot. It also shows how a civil conflict can become a global struggle.
The invasion of June 1950

On 25 June 1950 North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel into the South. They took Seoul within days. The UN Security Council called for help, and the United States led a UN force to defend South Korea. Historians argue about the start of the war. Soviet archives opened in the 1990s show that Kim Il Sung had won Stalin's approval for an attack, though Stalin wanted to avoid direct Soviet involvement.
Inchon and the march north

In September 1950 General Douglas MacArthur landed at Inchon, behind North Korean lines. The attack cut the enemy supply lines, and UN forces drove north. They reached the Yalu river, on the border with China, by late October. The advance triggered a Chinese intervention in October and November 1950. The Chinese army pushed back across the 38th parallel, and the war became a long, bloody stalemate.
Bruce Cumings and the origins

Bruce Cumings, The Korean War: A History (2010) Cumings argues that the origins of the war lay in the civil conflict within Korea and in the division of the country after 1945. He stresses that both sides had local goals. His view is controversial, but it is a useful correction to the simple picture of an invasion from nowhere.
The war in key dates
The war lasted three years and one month. The armistice line near the 38th parallel is still the basis of the demilitarised zone.
A stalemate at Panmunjom

Peace talks began in 1951 at Kaesong and later moved to Panmunjom. The talks dragged on for two years, mainly over the exchange of prisoners and the line of the front. Meanwhile the fighting continued, with trenches, hills and heavy losses. The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953. No peace treaty was ever signed, and the DMZ still divides the peninsula.
Was it a simple invasion?

The Korean War is often taught as a simple act of aggression by the communist North, stopped by the free world. The story is clear and easy to remember. Historians argue the picture is more complex. The Korean civil conflict, the Soviet and Chinese roles, the US decisions and the politics of the UN all shaped the war. Each side had its own reasons, and each made mistakes.
The cost of the war

Estimates of the dead run to about two to three million people, including civilians on both sides. Cities were destroyed, and many families were split by the border. The war left Korea divided and scarred. The war also changed the United States, which kept troops in Korea and Japan for decades. It helped set the pattern for the Cold War in Asia.
The forgotten war

The Korean War is often called the forgotten war, because it came between the Second World War and Vietnam. It received less attention in the West, though it was among the most intense conflicts of the Cold War. Historians argue about why the war is less remembered. The reasons include the late 1950s focus on other crises, and the lack of a clear victory. Its memory is strongest in Korea itself.
Prisoners and the choice of home

At the end of the war, many prisoners refused to return to the side that had held them. The question of repatriation nearly derailed the armistice. Over 20,000 prisoners chose not to go back to North Korea or China. The problem was handled by a neutral commission. It was the Indian army that took charge of the custody of the prisoners.
Meanwhile in India…

India played an unusual role in the Korean War. Krishna Menon, the Indian envoy at the UN, pushed for a compromise. In 1953 India agreed to chair a Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission and provided a custodian force to hold the prisoners. The Indian general K. S. Thimayya led the custodian force. The operation was a great test of neutrality in the Cold War. India's role showed how a newly independent country could shape world events.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The war ran from June 1950 to July 1953. Inchon (September 1950) turned the war. China entered in October 1950. The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. India chaired the prisoner repatriation commission. Think about it Why was the war never formally ended by a peace treaty? Can a neutral country do useful work in a war?
Vietnam: The Superpower's Longest Lost War
The superpower's longest lost war

The Vietnam War ran from the 1950s to 1975. The United States sent more than half a million troops at its height, and still lost. Its impact on America, Vietnam and the world remains deep. Vietnam is a warning about how a strong state can misread a war. It also shows the costs of a war fought for ideas, and of a war that divides a home country.
The French defeat

France tried to restore its rule over Indochina after the Second World War. The Viet Minh, led by Ho Chi Minh, fought the French from 1946. At Dien Bien Phu in 1954 the French army was defeated and forced to leave. The Geneva Accords of 1954 divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel. A communist north and an anti-communist south were meant to hold elections in two years, but the elections never took place.
From advisers to combat

The United States supported the government in Saigon with money and advisers. After the Gulf of Tonkin incident in August 1964, Congress gave the president wide powers, and the US sent combat troops in 1965. By 1969 the US had about 540,000 troops in Vietnam. Bombing campaigns and search-and-destroy operations failed to break the North Vietnamese and Viet Cong resistance.
Fredrik Logevall, Choosing War (1999)

Fredrik Logevall, Choosing War (1999) Logevall shows how US leaders in the early 1960s chose to commit to South Vietnam. He argues that the decisions were shaped by fear of looking weak and by Cold War thinking. The book is a key study of how the war was made, not only how it was fought.
The war in key dates
The war lasted almost thirty years when counted from the first French fights. For the Americans it lasted about a decade.
Tet 1968

In January 1968 the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese launched the Tet Offensive. They attacked more than a hundred towns and cities across South Vietnam, including the US embassy in Saigon. The attacks were defeated militarily, but they shocked the American public. Walter Cronkite and other reporters questioned whether the US could win. The offensive showed that the war could not be won quickly, and it helped turn US opinion against the war.
Was the war winnable?

Many people assume that the war was lost because of the press or the protests. Others argue the US could have won with more troops or different tactics. Both views are common. Historians argue that the war was shaped by the nationalism of the Vietnamese, the strength of the north and the mistakes of US planning. The idea that the media alone lost the war is not supported. The debate still shapes military thinking.
The end in Saigon

The Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 brought US troops home, but fighting continued. In April 1975 North Vietnamese tanks entered Saigon. The city was renamed Ho Chi Minh City, and the country was united under communist rule. Millions of Vietnamese had died in the war. Many fled as refugees, and the so-called boat people became a major issue in the late 1970s.
The costs

Estimates of the dead run to more than two million Vietnamese, including civilians, along with tens of thousands of Americans and large numbers of soldiers from South Vietnam and other allied forces. The bombing and the chemical defoliant Agent Orange left lasting scars. Historians argue about the numbers, which are uncertain. What is clear is that the war changed both countries and reshaped America's view of its own power.
Vietnam at home

In the United States, the war split families and campuses. Protests grew through the late 1960s, and young men faced the draft. The war became a central issue in American politics and culture. Veterans returned to a country divided over the war. Their experience, and the debate it created, still shapes American views of military power.
Meanwhile in India…

India was one of three members of the International Commission for Supervision and Control set up by the Geneva Accords of 1954. The commission, chaired by India, was to monitor the ceasefire and the division of the country. The Indian representatives reported the violations they saw, and they often found it hard to enforce the peace. India's role showed how a non-aligned country could try to mediate in a Cold War conflict, even when it had little power.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The French lost at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. The Geneva Accords divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel. The Gulf of Tonkin incident in 1964 led to US combat troops. The Tet Offensive of 1968 shocked US opinion. Saigon fell in April 1975. Think about it Why do strong states sometimes misread the strength of their enemies? How does a war at home change the way a war is fought abroad?
Partition of India in World Context
A line drawn in a few weeks

In August 1947 the British Raj ended, and British India was divided into two new states, India and Pakistan. Pakistan was made up of two wings, east and west, separated by over a thousand miles of Indian land. Partition was one of the largest and most violent migrations in modern history. It shaped the politics of South Asia for the rest of the century, and it remains a source of pain for millions of families.
Two nations and a British exit

The Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah demanded a separate homeland for Muslims. The Indian National Congress, led by Nehru and Patel, wanted a united India. Britain, under growing pressure after the Second World War, decided to leave by 1947. The Indian Independence Act was passed in July 1947. It set the date for independence at 15 August. Power was transferred to two dominions, and the princely states were left to choose their path.
The Radcliffe Line

The border between India and Pakistan was drawn by Cyril Radcliffe, a British barrister who had never been to India before. He had only a few weeks to draw the line through Bengal and Punjab. The final award was announced on 17 August 1947, two days after independence. Many people had no idea which country they would live in until the lines were published. Radcliffe's decision divided villages, canal systems and cities.
Urvashi Butalia and the other side of silence

Urvashi Butalia, The Other Side of Silence (1998) Butalia collected stories from families who lived through partition. She shows how women, children and village communities were affected, and how many people never spoke about the violence. Oral histories like this add a human layer to the political story.
Partition in key dates
The formal end of British rule was quick, but the social upheaval lasted for years. Millions moved across new borders in just a few months.
Migration and violence

Hindus and Sikhs moved from the west Punjab towards India. Muslims moved from India towards Pakistan. Trains, convoys and foot columns carried people in huge numbers, and many were attacked on the way. Estimates of the number of people who moved run to roughly ten to fifteen million. Estimates of those killed vary widely, from around two hundred thousand to over a million. Historians argue about the exact numbers.
Was partition inevitable?

Many textbooks treat partition as a natural result of religious difference that could not be avoided. The story suggests that two nations had always been separate. Historians argue that partition was the result of choices made by political leaders, the British and local crowds. Communal violence in the 1940s, the design of the British exit and the struggle for power all played a part. The idea of inevitability hides those choices.
Princely states

About 565 princely states had nominal independence within British India. Their rulers had to choose whether to join India or Pakistan. Hyderabad, Junagadh and Kashmir were the most contested. Hyderabad was taken over by Indian forces in 1948. Kashmir led to war between India and Pakistan in 1947 and 1948. The dispute is still unresolved and remains one of the most sensitive issues in South Asia.
Partition in world context

The partition of India was part of a wave of partitions after the Second World War. Ireland had been divided in 1921, and the UN recommended the partition of Palestine in November 1947. The pattern of drawing borders to meet political goals shaped much of the twentieth century. Historians compare the cases to see what they share. Partition often produced mass movements of people, and it often left a lasting legacy of conflict and memory.
Gandhi and the fast

Mahatma Gandhi opposed partition and worked for communal peace in Bengal and Delhi. In January 1948 he began a fast in Delhi to stop the violence. Later that month he was assassinated by a Hindu extremist, Nathuram Godse. Gandhi's death shocked India and the world. Historians argue about his role in the partition process, and his legacy in peace-making remains a strong part of public memory.
Two countries, one shared memory

Partition left two states with strong national identities and deep mistrust. Wars were fought in 1947, 1965, 1971 and 1999, and the Kashmir issue has never been settled. At the same time, shared language, food and music continue across the border. The memory of partition is kept alive in novels, films and family stories. It is one of the central events of the modern history of South Asia.
Meanwhile in India…

India became a republic in 1950, when its new Constitution came into force. The Constituent Assembly had begun its work in 1946 and included many voices from across the country, though it was dominated by Congress. The new state had to settle refugees, rebuild cities, and bring the princely states into the union. The Constitution's promise of equality was tested by the scale of the displacement and the violence.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember India and Pakistan became independent on 14 and 15 August 1947. Cyril Radcliffe drew the boundary line. Millions moved across the new border. Estimates of the dead vary widely. Kashmir remains disputed. Think about it Was partition a choice or a result of deeper forces? How should a nation remember a violent birth?
Apartheid: Engineering Racism in South Africa
A system built on the law

Apartheid was a system of racial laws that ruled South Africa from 1948 to the early 1990s. It classed people by race, separated them in homes and schools, and denied the black majority the vote. Apartheid is one of the clearest examples of how laws can build injustice. Its end is also one of the great stories of the 20th century.
The National Party wins in 1948

In 1948 the National Party, led by Afrikaner nationalists, won the white vote in South Africa. It promised to keep white rule and to separate the races more firmly. The word apartheid means "apartness" in Afrikaans. The party drew on fears about the growth of black cities and the political movements that were challenging segregation. It set out to make the system permanent through law.
The laws that built the system

The Population Registration Act of 1950 sorted every South African into a racial group. The Group Areas Act of 1950 forced people to live in separate areas. The Bantu Education Act of 1953 set up a separate school system with less money for black children. Black South Africans had to carry pass books, and many were forced into "homelands" or Bantustans, which were given a nominal independence. Millions were moved from their homes.
Gandhi in South Africa

Mohandas Gandhi in South Africa (1893–1914) Gandhi lived and worked in South Africa for over twenty years. He founded the Natal Indian Congress in 1894, and he developed satyagraha, or truth-force, as a tool of protest there. The Indian community of South Africa was one of the first targets of racial laws, and Gandhi's early struggles shaped his later methods.
Apartheid in key dates
The system grew over four decades. Its end came after mass protest, economic pressure and a changing world.
Sharpeville, 1960

On 21 March 1960 police fired on a crowd protesting against the pass laws at Sharpeville, south of Johannesburg. Sixty-nine people were killed, many of them shot in the back. The government banned the African National Congress and the Pan Africanist Congress. Sharpeville shocked the world. It led to international condemnation and helped turn many countries against South Africa, and it pushed the ANC toward armed struggle.
Was apartheid just segregation?

Apartheid is sometimes compared to the segregation of the American South, or treated as a version of ordinary racial separation. The comparison is common in teaching. Historians argue that apartheid was more than segregation. It was an attempt to engineer a racial society, with planned homelands, controlled movement and a system of laws designed to keep black South Africans without political rights. The scale of the state's control makes it unique.
Mandela and Rivonia

In 1963 police raided a farm in Rivonia and arrested the leaders of the armed wing of the ANC, Umkhonto we Sizwe. At the trial in 1964 Nelson Mandela spoke of his willingness to die for the ideal of a free society. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and spent 27 years in prison. Mandela's words became one of the most important statements of the anti-apartheid struggle. They also show how courage in court can shape a national story.
Soweto, 1976

On 16 June 1976 students in Soweto protested against the forced use of Afrikaans in schools. Police opened fire, and the uprising spread across the country. Hundreds were killed, and many young activists fled into exile. The uprising changed the struggle. It made a new generation of young leaders visible, and it forced the government to face the failure of its policies.
Sanctions and the end

International sanctions, divestment campaigns and the boycott of South African goods grew through the 1980s. Business and government leaders inside South Africa also came to see that apartheid could not last. Historians argue about how much each pressure mattered. The interplay of internal protest, the economy and the end of the Cold War made change possible. The end was not a single event but a long process.
Freedom in 1994

Nelson Mandela was released in February 1990. Negotiations led to a new constitution, and the first democratic elections were held in April 1994. The ANC won a large majority, and Mandela became the country's first black president. The transition was not peaceful in every place, but it avoided the civil war many had feared. The new South Africa was built on a constitution with a bill of rights.
Meanwhile in India…

When Gandhi returned to India in 1915, he carried his South African experience with him. Satyagraha became the core of the Indian freedom movement, and its methods inspired later struggles, including the civil rights movement in the United States and the anti-apartheid campaign. The link runs both ways. Indian activists in South Africa worked closely with African leaders, and Indian communities were among the victims of apartheid. Two movements, two countries, one shared language of protest.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The National Party came to power in 1948. The Population Registration Act sorted people by race in 1950. Sharpeville (1960) and Soweto (1976) were turning points. Mandela was sentenced in 1964 and released in 1990. The first democratic elections were held in 1994. Think about it How do laws create and then destroy a system of injustice? What made the end of apartheid possible?
The Iranian Revolution of 1979
A king is overthrown, a republic is born

In 1979 the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, fled the country. Within months the monarchy was replaced by an Islamic Republic led by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. The revolution changed Iran, the Middle East and Western policy for decades. It is one of the most important events of the late twentieth century. Its causes are still debated, and its effects are still felt in the region.
The Shah and his modernisation

The Shah ruled from 1941. In the early 1960s he launched the White Revolution, a programme of land reform, literacy drives and women's rights, paid for by oil revenue. Many of these changes were welcomed, but they also angered traditional clergy and the rural poor. The Shah relied on SAVAK, a feared secret police, to crush opposition. Critics said he was a dictator who ignored the people, and his court grew rich and distant.
Khomeini in exile

Khomeini had opposed the Shah since 1963 and was exiled in 1964. He lived in Turkey and Iraq, and from 1978 in France. From his exile he sent tapes and messages to Iran, and his speeches were copied and passed from hand to hand. His lectures in Najaf in 1970 argued for rule by Islamic jurists, the doctrine called velayat-e faqih. This became central to the republic he built after 1979.
Ervand Abrahamian, Iran Between Two Revolutions (1982)

Ervand Abrahamian (1982) Abrahamian argues that the 1979 revolution was a coalition. Clerics, students, merchants, workers and leftist groups all took part, and each had its own goals. He looks at the social roots of the protests and at how leaders built alliances across these groups. His book is a key counter to the view that the revolution was purely religious.
The revolution in key dates
The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979. Khomeini returned on 1 February. In April, a referendum set up the Islamic Republic.
Black Friday and the strikes

On 8 September 1978, soldiers fired on a huge crowd in Jaleh Square in Tehran. Many people were killed, and the day became known as Black Friday. Strikes spread through oil fields, banks and government offices in the autumn. The oil strikes hurt the state badly, because oil was its main source of income. By late 1978 the Shah's position was collapsing. His government fell to a wave of protest and desertion.
Was it purely a religious revolution?

Many Western accounts describe the revolution as a religious uprising led by mullahs. The image of the veiled crowd and the clerical leader dominates the story. Historians argue this view is too simple. Students, leftists, bazaar merchants and workers all played crucial roles. Khomeini was the leader who united them, but the revolution was not only a religious one. The later rule of the clergy narrowed its aims.
The hostage crisis

In November 1979 militant students stormed the US embassy in Tehran and took 52 Americans hostage. They were held for 444 days. The crisis dominated American politics, and it helped defeat President Jimmy Carter in 1980. The hostages were released on 20 January 1981, just as Carter left office. The crisis showed how deeply the revolution had shaken the relationship between Iran and the United States.
A republic built on clerical rule

The new constitution gave final authority to the leader, the supreme jurist, and created a Guardian Council to vet laws and candidates. Elections were held, but power lay with the clergy and with institutions they controlled. Historians argue whether the system is a democracy with religious limits or a religious state with elections. The answer depends on how you define democracy, and Iranians themselves still debate it.
A war with Iraq

In September 1980 Iraq invaded Iran. The Iran-Iraq War lasted until 1988 and killed hundreds of thousands. The war helped the new regime consolidate power, and it made the revolution's leaders see themselves as defending the nation. The war changed Iran's military and its foreign policy. It also left lasting debts and wounds on both sides.
Meanwhile in India…

In 1977 Indira Gandhi's Emergency, which had lasted since 1975, ended with her defeat in general elections. The Janata Party came to power in Delhi, a moment when democracy in India faced one of its hardest tests. Two very different revolutions and regime changes were happening in the same decade. In India, voters removed a leader from power at the ballot box. In Iran, a monarchy fell to a mass movement and a new clerical state.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979. Khomeini returned on 1 February 1979. Black Friday, 8 September 1978, was a turning point. The revolution was a coalition of groups. The US hostage crisis lasted 444 days. Think about it Can a revolution be both popular and authoritarian? Did the revolution fail, or did it succeed in its own terms?
Globalisation and the Internet Age
A steel box and a web page changed how the world trades and talks

In 1956 a trucker named Malcolm McLean loaded 58 metal containers onto a ship in New Jersey. It sounds dull. It made shipping so cheap that making a shirt in one country and selling it in another became normal. Then, in 1989-91, a scientist at CERN gave us the Web.
Boxes and borders
After the Cold War, trade barriers fell. The WTO started in 1995. China joined in December 2001 and became the 'world's factory'.
The Web

The Internet existed before the Web. Tim Berners-Lee , at CERN in Switzerland, proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 and it opened to the public in 1991. Google appeared in 1998 and Facebook in 2004. Smartphones, from 2007, put the Internet in billions of pockets.
Winners and losers

Globalisation lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, especially in Asia. But many factory workers in rich countries lost jobs, and inequality grew in many places. The 2008 financial crisis, then Brexit (2016) and trade wars, led many to ask if globalisation was going into reverse. Some call the new phase 'slowbalisation'.
Culture and data

Films, music, food and memes cross borders in seconds. Data became the new oil, and a few big firms hold a lot of it. Questions about privacy, misinformation and who controls the networks are now political issues.
Is globalisation brand new?

Myth: the world only got connected recently. Fact: the Silk Road, Indian Ocean trade and the Columbian Exchange were global. The 19th century saw a huge wave of trade too, which ended with World War I. What is new is the speed and the digital layer.
Meanwhile in India…

Reform, IT and UPI The 1991 reforms opened India to the world. Software firms like Infosys, founded in Bangalore in 1981, found a market in Y2K work in the late 1990s. India became a major exporter of IT services. In 2016 Jio made mobile data cheap. In April 2016 the National Payments Corporation of India launched UPI, which lets anyone send money from a phone. By 2023 it handled more than 10 billion transactions a month. Aadhaar, the ID system begun in 2009, made opening a bank account and signing up for a phone far easier, so millions went digital without ever holding a credit card.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Containers made trade cheap (1956). The Web went public in 1991. The WTO began in 1995; China joined in 2001. Gains were uneven. India's IT and digital payments rose after 1991. Think about it What do we lose if supply chains shrink? Who should control data?
9/11 and the War on Terror
The morning the world's news changed

On 11 September 2001, nineteen hijackers took four planes. Two struck the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, one hit the Pentagon, and one crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. Nearly 3,000 people died. It was the deadliest terror attack in history, and it launched two long wars.
Who did it?

The attack was carried out by al-Qaeda , led by Osama bin Laden , who had base camps in Afghanistan under the Taliban. Al-Qaeda had grown from the anti-Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s. It had already struck US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (1998).
Afghanistan, then Iraq
The US toppled the Taliban in weeks. In March 2003 it invaded Iraq, saying Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction. None were found.
A long war

The 'War on Terror' brought the Patriot Act, the Guantanamo prison and drone strikes. Bin Laden was found and killed by US forces at Abbottabad in Pakistan on 2 May 2011. In August 2021, after 20 years, US troops left Afghanistan and the Taliban retook Kabul on 15 August.
Costs and echoes

Hundreds of thousands died directly in the wars, with estimates varying by study. Millions were displaced. The Iraq war also helped create the space where ISIS grew. Terrorism continued in many countries, and debates about security and freedom reshaped airports and laws.
Did Saddam Hussein plan 9/11?

Myth: Iraq was behind the attacks. Fact: investigations (including the 9/11 Commission) found no operational link between Saddam's Iraq and the attacks. The WMD claim also proved false. Also: the Taliban's regime was separate from al-Qaeda, though it hosted it.
Meanwhile in India…

India had known terror already India was a victim of terror before 9/11. In March 1993 bombs in Mumbai killed about 250 people. In December 1999 an Indian Airlines flight, IC-814, was hijacked to Kandahar. On 13 December 2001, three months after 9/11, gunmen attacked Parliament in Delhi. On 26 November 2008 ten Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen from Pakistan attacked Mumbai for three days and killed more than 160 people. India argued for years that terror across its borders was a global problem. After 9/11 the world paid more attention, but India still struggled to win action against the groups based in Pakistan.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember 9/11 killed nearly 3,000. Al-Qaeda under bin Laden planned it. The US invaded Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2003). The Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021. India had also faced major attacks. Think about it How should states balance security and liberty? Why is defining terrorism so hard?
The Rise of China
A fishing town became a megacity in one generation

In 1980, Shenzhen near Hong Kong was a small market town of a few tens of thousands. Today it holds over 17 million people and makes much of the world's electronics. Shenzhen is the symbol of China's economic rise.
Deng opens the door

After Mao, Deng Xiaoping let farmers sell surplus crops, opened special economic zones and welcomed foreign investment. He is credited with the phrase about not caring if a cat is black or white if it catches mice (a saying he used).
The world's factory

With cheap labour and big ports, China exported huge quantities. After joining the WTO in 2001, growth soared, averaging near 10 percent a year for decades. China became the world's second-largest economy in 2010. The World Bank says about 800 million people in China left extreme poverty since 1978.
A different model

China combined one-party rule with market growth. The 'one-child policy' (1980-2015) cut births but left an ageing population. China's population began to shrink in 2022. Under Xi Jinping (leader since 2012-13), China launched the Belt and Road Initiative (2013), strengthened party control, and built a stronger navy.
Friction

Disputes arose over the South China Sea, Taiwan, trade and technology, and Hong Kong's 2020 National Security Law. The US sees China as its main rival. China argues it is reclaiming its place after the 'century of humiliation'. As of 2025, China remains the world's second-largest economy, but faces slowing growth and a property slump.
Is China's rise inevitable or fragile?

Some see unstoppable growth. Others point to debt, an ageing population and limited political freedom. Remember: China was the world's biggest economy for much of history before the 1800s, so many see this as a return. Caution: 'poverty reduction' numbers depend on the poverty line used.
Meanwhile in India…

Neighbours, rivals, partners China is India's neighbour, rival and partner. After the 1962 war, ties froze for years. In the 2000s trade grew fast. By 2023–24 China was India's largest trading partner, at about 118 billion dollars. Yet the border stayed tense. On 15 June 2020, in the Galwan valley in Ladakh, 20 Indian soldiers died in a clash. India banned many Chinese apps and tightened rules on investment. Modi and Xi met at Wuhan in 2018, and in October 2024 the two sides agreed on border patrolling arrangements. Both are in BRICS and both are rising, so the rivalry and the partnership continue side by side. Figures are as of 2024.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Reform began in 1978. Shenzhen and the WTO powered exports. China became No. 2 in 2010. Xi's China launched Belt and Road in 2013. India-China ties remain tense but linked. Think about it Is rapid growth possible without political freedom? How should India deal with a powerful neighbour?
Climate, Pandemics and the Shape of the Future
Two things changed everyday life in a way no army did

In March 2020, much of the world locked down within weeks because of a virus. And the same decade is on track to be the hottest in recorded history. This last lesson is about the stories still being written.
The warming planet

Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air. Earth has warmed by about 1.1-1.3 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s, according to major scientific bodies. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees, aiming for 1.5.
Effects

More heat waves, heavier rains, melting glaciers and rising seas. Poorer countries, which emitted least, often suffer most. Climate talks keep arguing over who should cut emissions and who should pay: this is the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities'.
COVID-19

The first cases were found in Wuhan in late 2019. The WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Vaccines using new mRNA technology arrived in under a year. The WHO estimated about 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-21, far higher than the 7 million officially reported. Pandemics are not new: the 1918 flu killed tens of millions.
New powers, new dangers

Artificial intelligence advanced quickly after 2022. Debates continue about jobs, deepfakes and control. Meanwhile, wars, trade rivalries and shifting power shape the global order. Nobody knows how it ends. History does not predict, but it gives you better questions.
Do scientists disagree about climate change?

Myth: scientists are split. Fact: studies find overwhelming agreement among climate scientists that humans are warming the planet. The real arguments are about speed, local effects and the best policies. Similarly, 'pandemics are one-offs' is wrong: experts expect more, which is why surveillance matters.
Meanwhile in India…

Solar, monsoon and vaccines India links climate and health to its own fate. The monsoon feeds its farms, but heatwaves and floods have grown worse. At COP26 in Glasgow in November 2021, India promised net zero emissions by 2070. In November 2015 Narendra Modi and France's François Hollande launched the International Solar Alliance in Paris. Its headquarters is in Gurugram, and it aims to bring cheap solar power to sunny countries. In the pandemic, the Serum Institute of India in Pune made Covishield, the AstraZeneca vaccine, under licence. From January 2021 India's Vaccine Maitri programme sent doses to dozens of countries, though a deadly second wave in April and May 2021 forced exports to pause.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Human emissions are warming Earth. Paris (2015) set the 1.5-2 degree goals. COVID-19 was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Climate and health are global, shared problems. India pledged net zero by 2070. Think about it Who should pay for climate action? Which lesson from history helps most with the future?
The Invention of the Internet
The network nobody planned

Today billions of people use the internet every day. Few stop to ask where it came from. The answer begins in the Cold War, with university labs, military research and a few people who had a new idea about how to send messages. The internet was not invented by one person or in one moment. It was built in layers, over decades, by many hands.
A bomb-proof network idea

In the early 1960s, the RAND researcher Paul Baran wrote about networks that could keep working even if parts were destroyed. At the same time, Donald Davies in Britain and Leonard Kleinrock in the United States worked on packet switching, which breaks messages into small pieces that travel separately. The idea was simple but radical. Messages would find their own way through the network, rather than following a fixed path like a phone call.
The first message, 1969

In October 1969 the first message was sent over ARPANET, the network funded by the US Defense Department's research agency. It went from a computer at UCLA to one at the Stanford Research Institute. The system crashed after the first two letters, so the first word was "lo". By the end of 1969 four university computers were linked. The network grew through the 1970s as researchers joined and shared files and email.
Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn

Cerf and Kahn (1974) In a paper published in 1974, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn described a protocol that could connect different networks. It became TCP/IP, the language that lets networks talk to each other. On 1 January 1983 the ARPANET switched fully to TCP/IP. Many historians mark that day as the birth of the internet as we know it.
The internet in key dates
The timeline shows how a military and academic network turned into a public one within a generation.
Tim Berners-Lee and the web

The internet and the web are not the same thing. The web is a system of linked pages and addresses that runs on the internet. In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN in Switzerland, proposed a system for sharing documents across the net. He wrote the first web browser and server in 1990. In 1991 the web was opened to the public, and it spread quickly, first in universities, then in homes.
Did Al Gore invent the internet?

A famous line from a 1999 interview suggests that Al Gore claimed to have invented the internet. The remark was widely mocked, and it has become a shorthand for political exaggeration. Historians argue that Gore had supported networking policy in Congress, but the internet was built by many scientists, engineers and institutions. Cerf and Kahn, Kleinrock and Berners-Lee each made key contributions. Credit is spread widely.
Public networks and money

In the 1980s and early 1990s the National Science Foundation built a backbone for academic networks, NSFNET. In 1991 the rules on commercial use were relaxed, and private companies began to offer dial-up internet to homes and businesses. Within a few years there were browsers, search engines and online shops. The internet became a commercial system as well as a research one.
Why the design matters

The internet was designed to be open. Its basic protocols do not control what people send. This design made it easy for new services to start, and it made it hard for any one company or state to control the whole network. Historians and lawyers argue about the costs of that openness, including spam, fraud and state surveillance. The design choices made in the 1970s still shape debates about privacy, speech and power.
A web of many languages

The early web was mostly in English. Over time it spread to other languages, and it now carries content in hundreds of scripts. Local languages and local content became a major part of the online world, especially in Asia and Africa. The shift shows how a technology built in one country can be remade by people elsewhere. It also raises questions about access, language and culture.
Meanwhile in India…

In 1995 the Indian company VSNL began offering commercial internet services, one of the first steps toward a public internet in India. Early users were mainly universities, research centres and a few businesses. Cheap mobile phones later pushed internet use far beyond the cities. By the 2020s hundreds of millions of Indians were online, and India had become one of the largest internet markets in the world.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Packet switching was developed in the 1960s. The first ARPANET message was sent in October 1969. TCP/IP was adopted on ARPANET in 1983. Tim Berners-Lee proposed the web in 1989. Commercial internet reached India in 1995. Think about it Who should get the credit for a shared invention? Does an open network make it harder to control speech?
Mandela and the Miracle of 1994
A prisoner who became a president

Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid. He walked out in 1990 and became South Africa's first democratically elected president in 1994. His story is one of the most famous of the modern world. Mandela's life also shows the hard choices of a freedom struggle: violence, negotiation, forgiveness and power. The lessons are still debated.
A young lawyer in Johannesburg

Mandela was born in 1918 in the Eastern Cape. He studied law and, in the 1940s, joined the African National Congress. In 1952 he helped lead the Defiance Campaign, in which volunteers broke apartheid laws in peaceful protest. Mandela was sometimes called the "Black Pimpernel" in the 1960s, for he moved in secret from place to place before his arrest. His early years show a man who first believed in disciplined, peaceful protest.
From protest to armed struggle

After Sharpeville in 1960, the ANC decided that peaceful protest alone would not work. In 1961 Mandela helped found Umkhonto we Sizwe, the armed wing of the movement. Its early campaign used sabotage against state targets, while avoiding deliberate killing of civilians. The decision was controversial, and historians still debate it. It shows how a movement can change its methods when peaceful protest is answered with force.
The Rivonia statement

Nelson Mandela at the Rivonia trial (1964) At the trial Mandela spoke for hours about the aims of the ANC and the reasons for its armed struggle. He ended with a famous line that he was prepared to die for the ideal of a free and democratic society. The speech is one of the most important political statements of the 20th century.
Mandela's long road
Mandela spent most of his adult life in prison or underground. His release came after years of pressure, and his election came after tough negotiations.
Robben Island

Mandela spent most of his imprisonment on Robben Island, off Cape Town. He worked in a lime quarry, where the glare damaged his eyesight. He studied, wrote letters and built a discipline among prisoners that became legendary. Prison changed him. He gained patience, and he learned to read his jailers. He also became a symbol for millions who had never met him.
Was Mandela a saint?

Mandela is often shown as a saint who forgave everything and never made mistakes. Monuments and speeches make him a figure of moral perfection. Historians argue that his life was more complicated. He led an armed movement, and his later government faced criticism for its economic policy and for the slow pace of land reform. Seeing him as a human leader gives a fuller picture than the saint image.
Negotiations and the 1994 vote

Negotiations between the ANC and the National Party, led by F. W. de Klerk, lasted several years. Both men shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. The first democratic elections, in April 1994, gave the ANC about 62 per cent of the vote, and Mandela took office in May. The new constitution included a bill of rights. The country faced huge problems of poverty, housing and inequality, but the peaceful transfer of power was a historic achievement.
Truth and reconciliation

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, heard testimony from victims and perpetrators between 1996 and 1998. It offered amnesty to those who told the full truth about political crimes. The commission is praised by some and criticised by others. Victims' families often felt justice was incomplete. Historians argue about its real effects, but its work remains a model studied around the world.
Power and restraint

Mandela served one term as president and then stepped down in 1999. He was one of the few African leaders of his era to leave office by choice, and he became an elder statesman who spoke on AIDS, poverty and peace. His restraint helped the new democracy take root. Historians argue about how much of that was personal and how much was built into the new system.
Meanwhile in India…

In 1991 India faced a serious balance-of-payments crisis. It borrowed from the IMF, and the government of P. V. Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as finance minister, began a programme of economic liberalisation. The two countries were both changing in the early 1990s. South Africa was moving from apartheid to democracy, and India was opening its economy to the world. Both made deep changes in the same years.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Mandela was sentenced to life in 1964 at the Rivonia trial. He was released in February 1990. The first democratic elections were held in April 1994. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission ran from 1996 to 1998. He stepped down after one term in 1999. Think about it Can a leader who once used violence become a symbol of peace? What does forgiveness owe to justice?
The Arab Spring: Hope and Its Aftermath
A wave that promised freedom

In late 2010 and 2011 protests spread across the Arab world. Dictators fell in Tunisia, Egypt and Libya. Other countries saw long conflicts or new repression. The events became known as the Arab Spring. The Arab Spring showed how quickly a region can change, and how hard it is to build a stable state after a revolution.
A fruit seller in Sidi Bouzid

On 17 December 2010 a young street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire in Sidi Bouzid, a town in central Tunisia, after police confiscated his goods. His death sparked protests that spread quickly across the country. The protests were about jobs, corruption and police abuse. Social media helped spread the images, but the anger came from long-running economic and political grievances.
Ben Ali flees, then Tahrir Square

Tunisia's president, Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, fled the country on 14 January 2011. In Egypt, huge crowds gathered in Tahrir Square in Cairo. President Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011 after weeks of protest. Egypt's revolution was a turning point. The square became a symbol of mass protest, and millions of people took part in marches across the country.
Marc Lynch on the new Arab politics

Marc Lynch, The Arab Uprising (2012) Lynch, a political scientist, argues that the uprisings were about dignity, politics and economic justice. He shows how the old regimes had depended on repression and patronage. His work helps explain both the hope of 2011 and the setbacks that followed.
The Arab Spring in key dates
The timeline shows how a wave of hope turned quickly into struggle, with different results in each country.
Libya and the war

In Libya, protests in February 2011 turned into civil war. NATO air forces supported rebel forces, and Muammar Gaddafi was killed in October 2011. The country then split between rival governments and armed groups for years. Historians argue about the role of outside intervention. Some say it saved lives. Others say it left Libya without a strong state and helped spread weapons across the region.
Was it a social media revolution?

Many accounts describe the Arab Spring as a revolution made by Facebook and Twitter. The phrase is catchy and has been repeated many times. Historians argue that technology mattered, but the uprisings were rooted in unemployment, food prices, corruption and repression. Social media spread the message faster, but it did not create the grievances. The story of the internet is only one part of the picture.
Syria and the long war

Protests in Syria began in March 2011, and the government responded with force. The protests became a civil war, with many armed groups, foreign powers and millions of refugees. The war has been one of the most devastating conflicts of the century. Syria shows how a peaceful protest can turn into a long war, and how regional and global powers can shape its course.
The Tunisian exception

Tunisia remained the most successful case. It adopted a new constitution in 2014 and held competitive elections. In 2015 the Tunisian National Dialogue Quartet, a group of unions and employers, won the Nobel Peace Prize for its role in the transition. Tunisia's path has also been fragile. Economic problems and political tensions have grown in recent years, and historians debate how durable its democracy will be.
Why did the wave break?

Historians offer several reasons for the setbacks. Old security forces stayed powerful, opposition movements were divided, and outside powers backed rival sides. In some countries the military took back control. The Arab Spring did not fail in every way. It changed what people expected from their governments, and it showed the limits of authoritarian rule. Its legacy is still being written.
Gulf money and regional rivals

Gulf states and regional powers backed different sides across the region. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates supported counter-revolution in several places, while Qatar and Turkey supported Islamist and rebel groups in others. The result was a region split by rivalries. This added to the conflicts in Libya, Syria and Yemen, and it made each country's transition harder.
Meanwhile in India…

In 2011, while the Arab world rose, India saw its own mass protests. Anna Hazare fasted at Jantar Mantar in Delhi to demand an anti-corruption law. Huge crowds gathered in cities across India, and the movement became one of the largest protests of the decade. India also had a large stake in the Arab world. Millions of Indians worked in the Gulf, and the Indian government evacuated thousands of its citizens from Libya in 2011 when the fighting began.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The protests began in Tunisia on 17 December 2010. Ben Ali left Tunisia in January 2011. Mubarak resigned in February 2011. Gaddafi was killed in October 2011. Tunisia's transition won the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize. Think about it Did the Arab Spring fail, or did it change expectations? How much do social media and economic anger each matter?
Aksum: Africa's Lost Empire
An empire that minted gold in Africa

Aksum was a kingdom in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea. From about the 1st to the 8th century CE it was one of the four great powers of the late ancient world, along with Rome, Persia and China. Aksum is often left out of world history. Its story shows how Africa was connected to the Mediterranean, Arabia and India long before the age of European exploration.
A port on the Red Sea

Aksum's wealth came from trade through its port of Adulis on the Red Sea. Ships carried ivory, gold and rhino horn out of Africa, and brought back textiles, glass, wine and olive oil from the Roman world. A 1st-century Greek sailing guide, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes the trade of Adulis. It shows that the port was busy with merchants from many lands.
King Ezana and the cross

King Ezana converted to Christianity in the 4th century, around the 330s CE. The monk Frumentius, from the Phoenician city of Tyre, who had been shipwrecked as a boy, served at the court and was later sent to Alexandria, where he was ordained as the first bishop of Aksum. Ezana's inscriptions, written in Ge'ez, Greek and Sabaean, mark his change of faith. Aksum became one of the earliest Christian kingdoms outside the Roman world.
The Ezana inscriptions

King Ezana's inscriptions (4th century CE) Ezana had stone inscriptions made in three languages. They describe his campaigns against peoples to the south and west, and they show a change from the older gods of Aksum to Christian faith. They are among the richest texts for early African history, and they are a key source for scholars of Aksum.
Aksum in key dates
Aksum rose on trade and faded as trade routes changed. Its decline came slowly, over centuries, and its capital moved inland.
Coins from Africa

Aksum minted its own coins in gold, silver and bronze. These were among the first coins in sub-Saharan Africa. They show a state with a sophisticated monetary system, and they carried the names and images of its kings. The coins were used in trade with the Roman world, Arabia and India. Their design changed over time, showing the state's shifting faith and power.
The great stelae

Aksum raised huge carved stone pillars, called stelae, some as tall as thirty metres. They mark royal tombs and were carved to look like multi-storey buildings. The largest fell and broke, and it was later returned from Italy to Ethiopia in 2005. The stelae show the skill of Aksumite stonemasons and the pride of its rulers. They are now among Ethiopia's most treasured monuments.
Is the Ark of the Covenant in Aksum?

Ethiopian tradition claims that the Ark of the Covenant is kept in a chapel in Aksum. It is a powerful story that links the city to the Bible. Scholars treat the claim as a religious tradition, not an historical fact. No outside researcher has been allowed to see the object, and it cannot be verified. The belief is important to Ethiopian Christians, but historians do not treat it as evidence.
Why did Aksum decline?

Aksum's trade was hit by the rise of new powers in Arabia and Iran, and the spread of Islam in the 600s and 700s changed Red Sea trade. The interior became more important, and the state moved its centre inland. Historians argue about the causes. Some stress climate change and drought, others point to changing trade routes and the rise of new cities. The decline was a slow shift rather than a sudden collapse.
A Christian kingdom in Africa

Aksum was one of the earliest Christian states in the world. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church traces its roots to the Aksumite kings and the early bishops. This long Christian tradition still shapes Ethiopian identity. Ethiopia was never fully colonised by a European power, except for a brief Italian occupation in the 1930s. Historians often point to Aksum's long history as part of that independence.
Meanwhile in India…

In the 4th century the Gupta empire was minting gold coins in India, as Aksum was minting its own gold. The two kingdoms were on opposite ends of the Indian Ocean trade system. Indian cloth and spices moved through the Red Sea ports, and Aksum's traders were part of the same network. Coins from both kingdoms show how trade could link distant states.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Aksum was based in the northern Ethiopian highlands. Its port was Adulis on the Red Sea. King Ezana converted to Christianity around the 330s. Aksum minted its own gold, silver and bronze coins. Its decline came slowly, from the 600s onward. Think about it Why is Aksum often left out of world history? The Hanseatic League: Trade Without Kings
Trade without a king

From the 1200s to the 1600s, merchant towns across northern Europe formed a loose network called the Hanseatic League. It had no king, no army of its own and no single capital. Yet it shaped trade from London to Novgorod. The Hanseatic story shows how commerce, city law and shared rules could build a power that rivalled kings.
Lübeck and the merchants

The city of Lübeck, on the Baltic coast of northern Germany, was the centre of the League. Its merchants developed trade rules and a shared legal code, the Lübeck law, which was copied by many towns. Hamburg, Bremen and Danzig became important partners. The League met in assemblies called Hansetage. Member towns decided on common rules, trade privileges and, when needed, joint action against rivals.
Trade posts across Europe

The Hanseatic merchants ran trading posts, called kontors, in key cities. These included the Steelyard in London, the Peterhof in Novgorod, the Bryggen in Bergen and a post in Bruges. The posts were like small walled communities with their own rules. The kontors gave the League control over the trade in fish, grain, timber, furs and wax. Bergen's dried cod and Baltic grain flowed through the same network.
Philippe Dollinger and the German Hansa

Philippe Dollinger, The German Hansa (1964) Dollinger's classic study shows how the League worked in practice. He describes the trade routes, the member towns and the disputes that shaped their policy. The book is still a standard guide, although later historians have added many new views.
The Hanseatic League in key dates
The League was at its strongest in the 14th and 15th centuries. Its decline came as new states and new trade routes took its place.
War with Denmark

In the 1360s the League fought a war against King Valdemar IV of Denmark, who had taken control of Scania and threatened Baltic trade. The League won, and the 1370 Peace of Stralsund gave its members new trading privileges. The war showed that the League could act as a naval and political power. It could choose kings and make peace, even without a single state behind it.
Was the Hanseatic League a state?

Many people picture the League as a kind of medieval state, with a government and an army. The idea makes it easier to compare with modern nations. Historians argue that the League was an association of towns and merchants, with shared rules but no central authority. Its members were often rivals. It is better described as a network than as a country.
Fish, grain and furs

Bergen's dried cod was sent south to feed Catholic Europe on fast days. Baltic grain and timber fed growing cities in the west, and furs and wax came from the eastern forests. Each good had its own trade route and its own rules. The trade was profitable and organised. The Hanseatic merchants were shrewd, and they controlled the sale and quality of their goods with strict rules.
Why did the League decline?

The League faded from the 1500s to the 1600s. Some historians point to the rise of strong territorial states, such as Sweden, Denmark and Russia, that controlled trade themselves. Others point to the shift of trade to the Atlantic. The decline was gradual. Historians argue about the causes, but the League never completely vanished, and the names of its cities still mark the Hanseatic past.
Lübeck and Novgorod

The Peterhof in Novgorod was a major Hanseatic base. Russian princes allowed the merchants to trade there, and the merchants shipped furs, wax and honey to the West. The link was an early sign of Russia's place in European trade. The relationship was not always peaceful. Disputes over rights and justice were common, and both sides used the courts to protect their interests.
Meanwhile in India…

In 1329 the Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a copper token currency. The coins were meant to replace silver, but they were easy to forge, and trade collapsed. The king had to withdraw the tokens. The Hanseatic towns were built on silver and trust. Muhammad's token money failed because people did not trust the paper of the state. The contrast shows how much coinage depended on confidence.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The League was a network of merchant towns, not a state. Lübeck was its centre. Kontors in London, Bergen, Bruges and Novgorod were its trading bases. The 1370 Peace of Stralsund gave it new privileges. It faded from the 1500s to the 1600s. Think about it Can a network of towns be as powerful as a king? What holds a trading alliance together when it has no army?
The Library of Alexandria
The library that became a legend

The Library of Alexandria, in Egypt, was one of the most famous places of learning in the ancient world. It was part of a research centre called the Mouseion, and it collected scrolls from across the Mediterranean. Its story is part fact and part legend. The question of what was lost, and why, still fascinates readers and historians.
Ptolemy and the book collection

The Ptolemaic kings of Egypt founded the library around 300 BCE, under Ptolemy I or Ptolemy II. They bought and copied books and sent ships to borrow scrolls from other cities. Some books were said to be taken from visitors who were searched. The library grew to hold many hundreds of thousands of scrolls at its height, though the exact number is uncertain. It was a place where scholars from around the Mediterranean lived and worked.
Scholars of the Mouseion

Scholars at Alexandria made major advances. Eratosthenes, who ran the library, measured the size of the Earth by comparing shadows in Alexandria and Syene. Euclid, who taught mathematics there, wrote his Elements, which shaped geometry for centuries. The city was a place of debate, poetry and medicine. Its scholars edited Homer, catalogued literature and studied the stars.
Strabo on the Mouseion

Strabo (c. 64 BCE – c. 24 CE) The Greek geographer Strabo visited Alexandria and described the Mouseion. He wrote of its shared dining hall, its scholars and their salaries paid by the state. His account is one of the few eyewitness descriptions of the institution.
Alexandria's library through time
The library did not disappear in one night. It faded over centuries, through wars, neglect and changing priorities.
Did Caesar burn the library?

A popular story says that Julius Caesar set fire to the library in 48 BCE and destroyed its books. The image of a great fire is dramatic and widely repeated. Historians argue the fire was real but limited. Roman writers mention books being lost in fighting near the harbour. The library may have survived for centuries after that, so the single fire story is probably exaggerated.
The Caliph and the baths

A later legend claims that the Caliph Omar ordered the books burned as fuel for the city's baths. The story appears in writings of the 1200s, centuries after the events. Historians treat it as a legend, not a record. The legend shows how later writers used the library as a symbol. It is a warning about the fragility of knowledge.
Copies that kept texts alive

Much of the ancient world we know survives through copies made in Alexandria. Scholars there created standard texts of Homer and the tragedians, and their editions helped preserve the Greek literary canon. Historians argue that the real loss was not one fire, but the slow decline of funding, copying and interest over centuries. What survived depended on luck and on a few people who kept copying.
The Serapeum and the end

The Serapeum, a temple in Alexandria that held a daughter library, was destroyed in 391 CE during a campaign against pagan sites. Some books may have been lost then, though the evidence is limited. By the time of the Arab conquest in 642, the library was no longer the great institution it had been. The question of how much was lost is still open.
The idea of a universal library

The Library of Alexandria became a model for later collections, from the libraries of Baghdad and Cordoba to modern national libraries. Its ideal of gathering all knowledge in one place still inspires projects today. The lesson is double-edged. The ideal of a universal collection is powerful, but it depends on money, politics and the survival of institutions.
Meanwhile in India…

Alexandria's Ptolemies were in contact with India. Ashoka's rock edicts, carved in the mid-200s BCE, name Greek kings in the west who received Buddhist envoys, among them a ruler called Ptolemy. So the library was one node in a wider world of exchange. Greek learning and Indian religion met in the same century, and both left records of the contact.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The library was part of the Mouseion, a research centre. The Ptolemies founded it around 300 BCE. Eratosthenes measured the Earth using shadows. The fire of 48 BCE was real but limited. The story of Omar burning the books is a later legend. Think about it Why do lost libraries become legends? What makes a body of knowledge survive for centuries?
Dunhuang: The Caves That Saved a Library
A library hidden in a cliff

In 1900 a Daoist monk named Wang Yuanlu found a sealed room behind a wall in the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang, on the Silk Road in northwest China. Inside were tens of thousands of manuscripts, written over centuries. The discovery changed what we know about Buddhism, Chinese history and the Silk Road. It is still one of the great finds of modern scholarship.
Caves carved for the Buddha

The Mogao Caves were carved from the cliffs from about 366 CE onward, according to tradition. Over the next thousand years monks, donors and artists painted murals and built statues. The caves became a major centre of Buddhist art. Dunhuang sat where roads from China split into northern and southern routes across the Taklamakan desert. Merchants, monks and pilgrims all passed through.
A sealed room

The library cave, known as Cave 17, was sealed up around the 11th century. The reasons are unclear. Some think it was done to protect the texts from danger, others think the monks simply abandoned the site. When Wang Yuanlu opened it in 1900, he found manuscripts in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Uighur and other languages. Many were Buddhist scriptures, but there were also letters, contracts and popular songs.
The Diamond Sutra of 868

The Diamond Sutra (868 CE) One scroll found in the cave is a printed copy of the Diamond Sutra, dated 868 CE. It is the earliest dated printed book known, made with woodblocks and a colophon with the date. It is now in the British Library, and it is often shown as a landmark in the history of print.
Dunhuang in key dates
The timeline runs from the first caves to the modern collectors who carried the manuscripts away.
Aurel Stein and the Western collectors

In 1907 the Hungarian-born British explorer Aurel Stein bought a large number of manuscripts from Wang. The following year the French scholar Paul Pelliot also collected many texts. Their works now sit in London, Paris, Beijing and other cities. The purchases were controversial then and remain so now. Many Chinese scholars see the removals as a loss of national heritage, while others argue that the texts were preserved better in libraries abroad.
Did Wang Yuanlu sell the treasures for a pittance?

A common story says that Wang sold the library for small sums and that he did not understand what he had. The image makes him a villain or a fool, and it is widely repeated. Historians argue the story is partly true and partly unfair. Wang did sell texts for money, and he was not a scholar. But he also tried to protect the site and to report his find. The real picture of his choices is complex.
What the library tells us

The Dunhuang texts include sutras, histories, medical texts, calendars and songs. They show the variety of life at a Silk Road city. Some texts give voices to ordinary people, such as merchants, women and soldiers. Historians argue that the library is a snapshot of a border region, not a full picture of China. Its strange mix of texts is valuable precisely because it does not fit neatly into one tradition.
Kumarajiva's translation

The Diamond Sutra was originally a Sanskrit text. The monk Kumarajiva, who came from the Silk Road city of Kucha, translated it into Chinese around 402 CE. That translation was copied and spread across East Asia. The text is a Buddhist teaching about emptiness and illusion. Its message reached far beyond the caves and helped shape Chinese Buddhism.
A place of many languages

The Dunhuang manuscripts were written in more than a dozen languages, including Tibetan, Uighur, Khotanese and Sogdian. They show the reach of Silk Road networks and the mixing of cultures in a border city. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site today. Its caves and manuscripts show how a border town can hold the memory of an entire trade world.
Meanwhile in India…

The Diamond Sutra was a Sanskrit text from India. Its message came to China through monks and translators, and the Silk Road carried Indian Buddhist ideas across Central Asia. Dunhuang shows that link in paper and paint. Indian monks, artists and teachers were part of the same world of exchange. The caves show Indian themes, such as stories of the Buddha, carried to China along the route.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Mogao Caves near Dunhuang hold a sealed library. Wang Yuanlu found it in 1900. The Diamond Sutra printed in 868 is the earliest dated printed book known. Stein and Pelliot took many manuscripts abroad. The texts are in many languages, including Sanskrit and Tibetan. Think about it Who should own a heritage found in one country but written by many peoples? What makes a text worth keeping?
